citations.quote: **(i) The two-label central model.** A model of class (i) is a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$ labels, fixed masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_0$, the collision-excluded configuration domain $$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$ for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and the force map presented through the time-independent **static central pair potential** $$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),\qquad u:J_0\to\mathbb R\ \text{of class }C^2,$$ so that $F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain (clauses (iii) and (iv) of [[post-cm02-interactions]]; $U$ is of class $C^2$ on the open $Q$ by [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). In the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of that postulate the model has $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$: no external forces act on the labels of a model of class (i).

4. **(Reconstruction and bijection.)** The identities $x_1=X+\frac{m_2}{M}r$ and $x_2=X-\frac{m_1}{M}r$ hold on $J$. Conversely, if $X^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is affine with $(X^{\circ})''=0$ and $r^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is a $C^2$ curve with $\lvert r^{\circ}(t)\rvert\in J_0$ and $\mu(r^{\circ})''=-u'(\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert)r^{\circ}/\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert$ on $J$, then $$x_1^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}+\frac{m_2}{M}r^{\circ},\qquad x_2^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}-\frac{m_1}{M}r^{\circ}$$ define a motion $x^{\circ}:J\to Q$ of the model whose centre of mass is $X^{\circ}$ and whose relative coordinate is $r^{\circ}$. Consequently the assignment $x\mapsto(X,r)$ is a bijection from the motions of the model on $J$ onto the pairs (affine curve $X^{\circ}$ with $(X^{\circ})''=0$\!, central-force trajectory $r^{\circ}$ for $(\mu,u)$ with values in $J_0$) on $J$.

The curve $r$ is a **central-force trajectory for** $(\mu,U)$ when $$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{U'(|r(t)|)}{|r(t)|}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in I),$$ where $|x|:=\lVert x\rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and $U'$ is the derivative of $U$ on the open interval $J_0$. **Attached objects.** The **angular momentum vector** of such a trajectory is the curve $j:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $$j(t):=\mu\,r(t)\times r'(t),$$ with $\times$ the cross product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); its **energy** is the function $E:I\to\mathbb R$, $$E(t):=\tfrac12\mu\,\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2+U(|r(t)|);$$ and for every $J\ge0$ the **effective potential of momentum magnitude** $J$ is the function $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J:J_0\to\mathbb R$, $$U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho):=U(\rho)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu\,\rho^2}.$$

**(a) Unconstrained branch.** The **unconstrained configuration domain** is an open set $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, chosen as part of the model. A tuple $x\in Q$ is an **admissible configuration**: an assignment of one position to each label at one time. A **singular-force exclusion** is the removal of the **collision set** $$\Delta:=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:\ \text{there are }i\ne j\text{ with }x_{i}=x_{j}\Bigr\}$$ from the domain, which is done when the model's force law is not defined at coincident positions: $\Delta$ is closed (it is the union of the finitely many closed sets $\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}$, each the zero set of the continuous map $x\mapsto x_{i}-x_{j}$), so $Q:=\mathbb R^{3N}\setminus\Delta$ is open and is a legitimate configuration domain.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in [[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that $t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and $$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$ Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to D$ is a solution of the associated first-order system on $J$.

Let $\mu>0$, let $U:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ be of class $C^2$, let $R>0$ satisfy $U(r)=0$ for every $r\ge R$, let $E>0$ and $J>0$, and put $V(r):=U(r)+J^2/(2\mu r^2)$ ([[def-cm-scattering-data]]). Suppose $r_*>0$ satisfies $$V(r_*)=E,\qquad V'(r_*)<0,\qquad V(r)<E\quad(r>r_*).$$ Let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant nonzero angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, energy $E$, and $|r(t)|\ge r_*$ for all $t\in I$, whose radial part attains the value $r_*$ at some $t_*\in I$ ([[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]). Then: 1. $(\rho')^2=\dfrac{2}{\mu}\bigl(E-V(\rho)\bigr)$ on $I$, where $\rho=|r|$; $\rho'(t_*)=0$ and $\rho''(t_*)=-V'(r_*)/\mu>0$, so $t_*$ is a strict minimum of $\rho$; 2. $r$ extends uniquely to a central-force trajectory on all of $\mathbb R$; along the extension $\rho\ge r_*$, $\rho(t)>\rho(t_*)=r_*$ for $t\ne t_*$, and $\rho$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$; 3. the time quadrature $$\tau(r):=\int_{r_*}^{r}\frac{\mathrm ds}{\sqrt{(2/\mu)(E-V(s))}} \qquad(r\ge r_*)$$ is finite for every $r$ and satisfies $\rho(t_*+\tau(r))=r$ for all $r\ge r_*$; 4. for every time $t_1\ge t_*$ with $\rho(t_1)>R$ the motion is exactly free from $t_1$ on: $r(t)=r(t_1)+(t-t_1)r'(t_1)$ for all $t\ge t_1$, and $\rho$ is strictly increasing there; symmetrically, for $t_2\le t_*$ with $\rho(t_2)>R$, $r(t)=r(t_2)+(t-t_2)r'(t_2)$ for all $t\le t_2$.

Let the hypotheses of [[thm-cm-scattering-turning-point-and-global-branches]] hold, with finite-range potential $U$, energy $E>0$, angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, outer turning point $r_*$, and let $r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be the extension of the trajectory. Then: 1. the limits $v_\pm:=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r'(t)$ exist and satisfy $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$; 2. for every $t_2\le t_*$ with $\rho(t_2)>R$, the incoming branch is the straight line $\{r(t_2)+s\,v_-:s\in\mathbb R\}$; its perpendicular distance from the origin is $$b:=\frac{|r(t_2)\times v_-|}{|v_-|}=\frac{J}{\mu|v_-|}, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad J=\mu b|v_-| .$$

Then: 1. the half-angle $$\Delta:=\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu\,(E-V(r))}}$$ is finite and positive, and $$\theta(\infty)-\theta(t_*)=\Delta=\theta(t_*)-\theta(-\infty),\qquad \theta(\infty)-\theta(-\infty)=2\Delta;$$ 2. $\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}n(\theta(t))$ exist and equal $v_+/|v_+|$ (as $t\to+\infty$) and $-v_-/|v_-|$ (as $t\to-\infty$); 3. consequently $$\frac{v_+}{|v_+|}=-R_{2\Delta}\Bigl(\frac{v_-}{|v_-|}\Bigr), \qquad \frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{|v_-|\,|v_+|}=-\cos 2\Delta=\cos(\pi-2\Delta);$$ in particular, if $0<\Delta<\pi/2$ then $\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi)$ is the (undirected) angle between the asymptotic velocity directions, and the signed velocity rotation is $-( \pi-2\Delta)$ in the orientation defined by $e_3$.

Let $(a_1,a_2)\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an interval with at least two points, let $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ be of class $C^1$ with $\theta'(b)\ne0$ for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$ — a deflection branch with inverse $b:(\theta_1,\theta_2)\to(a_1,a_2)$ in the sense of [[def-cm-scattering-data]] — and let $g:(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and $2\pi$-periodic in its second argument. Then $$\int_{a_1}^{a_2}\!\int_0^{2\pi} g\bigl(\theta(b),\varphi\bigr)\,b\;\mathrm db\;\mathrm d\varphi =\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(\theta,\varphi)\,b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|\;\mathrm d\theta\;\mathrm d\varphi .$$ Consequently the outgoing angular measure carried to the branch has density $b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|$ with respect to $\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi$, and cross-section density $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta) =\frac{b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'(b(\theta))\bigr|}\qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2)$$ with respect to the solid-angle element $\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi$; the two expressions agree because $b'(\theta)=1/\theta'(b(\theta))$. For finitely many branches with pairwise disjoint images the contributions add.

**Deflection branch.** A **deflection branch** is an interval $(a_1,a_2)\subseteq(0,\infty)$ with at least two points together with a function $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ that is of class $C^1$ and satisfies $\theta'(b)\ne0$ for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$. Such a $\theta$ is strictly monotone and its image is an interval with endpoints $\theta_1<\theta_2$ ([[def-interval]]); its inverse $b:(\theta_1,\theta_2)\to(a_1,a_2)$ is differentiable with $b'(\theta)=1/\theta'(b(\theta))$, by the derivative-of-an-inverse theorem [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]] applied to the continuous injective $\theta$ (every point of $(a_1,a_2)$ is a limit point of it, [[def-limit-point-r]], [[def-derivative]]). **Cross-section density.** The **cross-section density of the branch** is the function $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|} \qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2).$$

**(i) The differential cross-section of a branch.** Let a central scattering model be given, let $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ be a **deflection branch** in the sense of [[def-cm-scattering-data]] — an interval $(a_1,a_2)$ of impact parameters with $\theta$ of class $C^1$ and $\theta'(b)\ne0$ — and suppose the branch **records the deflection** of the model: for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$ the scattering motion of the model with impact parameter $b$, energy $E$ and angular momentum $J$ has scattering angle $\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\theta(b)$. Write $(a_1,a_2)\ni b\mapsto\theta\in(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ for this bijection and $b(\theta):=\theta^{-1}(\theta)$ for its inverse ([[def-cm-scattering-data]]). The **differential cross-section of the branch** is the function $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|}\qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2),$$ the cross-section density of [[def-cm-scattering-data]].

**(iv) The uniform-incident preparation (adopted model datum).** The **uniform-incident preparation** of a central scattering model with cutoff $b_{\max}>0$ and flux $\Phi>0$ is the following adopted model of a scattering experiment for the reduced problem: independent incident reduced labels, each with energy $E>0$, angular momentum $Je_3$ and impact-azimuth pair distributed with density $b\,\mathrm db\,\mathrm d\varphi$ on $(0,b_{\max})	imes(0,2\pi)$ normalised to unit total mass, where the **incident flux** $\Phi$ is the number of incident labels per unit area per unit time and $[\Phi]=\ell^{-2}	au^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). Under this preparation the model predicts the expected rate $$\dot N(A)= \Phi\cdot
u(A)$$ of incident labels whose impact-azimuth pair lies in $A$, where $
u$ is the incident flux measure of [[def-cm-scattering-data]]; the rate of scattered labels into a solid-angle set is the flux times the pushforward of $
u$ under the deflection map, whose density on a branch is the cross-section density introduced in this page's cross-section definition.
For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$. This is the right-handed **cross product**.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The **Euclidean norm** of $x$ is $$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$ which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and [[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by [[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function $$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$ the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ ([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives $x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$. $f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in $\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is $$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$: | | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms | |---|---|---|---| | $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ | | $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ | | $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ | | $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ | | | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is **closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$, $[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

### Limits, for a real domain Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$, let $c$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. We say $f(x)$ **tends to $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$**, and write $\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$, when $$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ 0 < |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ \lVert f(x) - L\rVert_2 < \varepsilon\ \bigr].$$ This is the condition of [[def-function-limit]] with the absolute value in the codomain replaced by $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$; as there, the puncture $0 < |x-c|$ is what makes $c$ a point the function need not be defined at, and the hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is what stops the condition from being satisfied vacuously.

derivations.claim: The relative coordinate is a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ with attached angular momentum $j=Je_3$ and energy $E$ by [L1], of class $C^2$ with values $|r(t)|\in J_0=(0,\infty)$; thus $r$ satisfies all hypotheses of the finite-range scattering theorems [L2] with the data $(\mu,u,R,E,J,r_*)$: $U=u$ is $C^2$ on $(0,\infty)$, $U(r)=0$ for $r\ge R$ by (H1), $V(r_*)=E$ with $V'(r_*)<0$ and $V(r)<E$ for $r>r_*$ by (H2), and the trajectory attains the value $r_*$ at $t_*\in J_0$ while satisfying $|r|\ge r_*$.

Clause 1: [L2] gives that $r$ extends uniquely to a central-force trajectory $\bar r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ with $\rho\ge r_*$, $\rho(t)>r_*$ for $t\ne t_*$, $\rho$ strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$, and the quadrature identity. For the model statement, let $X$ be the centre of mass of the original motion, affine on $J_0$ with $X''=0$ by [L1] clause 2, and let $\bar X$ be its affine extension to $\mathbb R$; then by [L1] clause 4 the pair $(\bar X,\bar r)$ reconstructs a motion of the model on all of $\mathbb R$ with relative coordinate $\bar r$ and centre of mass $\bar X$, because $|\bar r(t)|\in J_0$ for all $t$ (so the configuration remains admissible) and the force presentation is the same. This is clause 1.

Clause 2, asymptotic velocities: by [L2] the limits $v_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}\bar r'(t)$ exist with $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}=v_\infty>0$, and for every $t_1\ge t_*$ with $\rho(t_1)\ge R$ one has $\bar r(t)=\bar r(t_1)+(t-t_1)\bar r'(t_1)$ for $t\ge t_1$, with $\bar r'(t_1)=v_+$; the incoming statement is symmetric.

Clause 3: by [L2] the half-angle identity $\theta(+\infty)-\theta(t_*)=\Delta=\theta(t_*)-\theta(-\infty)$ holds with $\Delta$ the displayed finite positive quadrature, and the directional identities $v_+/|v_+|=-R_{2\Delta}(v_-/|v_-|)$ and $\langle v_-,v_+\rangle/(|v_-||v_+|)=\cos(\pi-2\Delta)$ hold; hence $\theta_{\mathrm s}=\arccos(\cos(\pi-2\Delta))$ by the definition of $\theta_{\mathrm s}$ in [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] clause (iii), and if $0<\Delta<\pi/2$ then $\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi)$ is that angle, the signed velocity rotation being $2\Delta-\pi$. This is clause 3.

Clause 2, impact parameter: on the incoming branch choose $t_2\le t_*$ with $\rho(t_2)\ge R$; the incoming line is $\{\bar r(t_2)+s\,v_-:s\in\mathbb R\}$ and its perpendicular distance from the origin is $|\bar r(t_2)\times v_-|/|v_-|=|j|/(\mu|v_-|)=J/(\mu v_\infty)$ by [L2] clause 2 and [L4]. For the outgoing line $\{\bar r(t_1)+s\,v_+:s\in\mathbb R\}$, the same computation with [L4] gives distance $|\bar r(t_1)\times v_+|/|v_+|=|j|/(\mu|v_+|)=J/(\mu v_\infty)$; since $J/(\mu\sqrt{2E/\mu})=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}$, both distances equal $b=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}$ as displayed, and multiplying by $v_\infty$ gives $J=\mu b v_\infty$.

Clause 4: by the branch hypothesis the model's scattering angle at impact parameter $b\in(a_1,a_2)$ equals $\theta(b)$, and $\theta$ is a deflection branch with inverse $b(\theta)$; [L3] then gives the displayed double-integral identity and the density statements, the cross-section density agreeing with the definition of [[def-cm15-cross-section]] clause (i). For the expected rate, the uniform-incident preparation assigns incident flux measure $\nu$ with density $b$ on $(0,b_{\max})\times(0,2\pi)$ and the model predicts the rate $\Phi\,\nu(A)$ of labels with impact-azimuth data in $A$ and, for the branch, the pushforward rate into the window $Y=(\theta(a_1),\theta(b_{\max}))$; expressing that pushforward through the density of [L3] and converting the polar measure $\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi$ into the solid-angle element gives $\Phi\sigma(Y)$ with $\sigma$ as displayed in [[def-cm15-cross-section]] clause (iii). This is clause 4.

Clause 5 is the statement of the scope: the branch hypothesis of clause 4 is an explicit assumption, not a consequence of (H1)-(H2); no monotonicity or nonvanishing of $\theta'$ off the branch is used or claimed; and the exclusions are those of [[post-cm05-central-model]] clause (v) together with (H1). This completes the proof.

boundaries.evidence: The branch interval is nondegenerate by the definition of a deflection branch, and step 3.2 applies the area pushforward on it; no possibly empty family is quantified.
$E>0$ and $J>0$ exclude the zero-energy and radial cases in step 1.1, and the branch derivative is nonzero by hypothesis in step 3.2.
One relative coordinate, one apsis and one branch in clause 4; step 3.1 computes the single number $b=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}$ on both asymptotes.
The simple outer turning point $V'(r_*)<0$ of (H2) is checked in step 1.1, and stationary deflections $\theta'(b)=0$ are excluded from the branch in step 3.2.
The improper endpoint $r_*$ of the quadrature is finite by clause 1 (step 2.1); the branch image endpoints are excluded from the density and the cutoff may equal the upper endpoint (step 3.2).

citations.quote: Let $\mu>0$, let $\kappa>0$ and $U(r)=\kappa/r$ on $(0,\infty)$ (the repulsive Coulomb potential, of class $C^2$), let $E>0$ and $J>0$, and put $$V(r):=\frac{\kappa}{r}+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2},\qquad b:=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}>0,\qquad \alpha:=\frac{\kappa}{Eb}>0.$$ Then: 1. $V$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,\infty)$, with $V(r)\to\infty$ as $r\downarrow0$ and $V(r)\to0$ as $r\to\infty$; hence there is exactly one $r_*>0$ with $V(r_*)=E$, it is simple ($V'(r_*)<0$), and $V(r)<E$ for all $r>r_*$. 2. Let $r:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,U)$ with constant angular momentum $j=Je_3$, $J>0$, energy $E$, with $|r(t)|\ge r_*$ for all $t\in I$ and with $|r(t_*)|=r_*$ for some $t_*\in I$. Then $r$ extends uniquely to all of $\mathbb R$; along the extension $\rho=|r|\ge r_*>0$ (no collision), $\rho$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$, and the asymptotic velocities $v_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}r'(t)$ exist with $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$. Moreover the asymptotic perpendicular distance of each branch to its limiting direction exists and equals $$b=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}}=\frac{J}{\mu|v_\pm|}, \qquad\text{so that}\qquad J=\mu b|v_\pm| .$$ 3. For the polar angle, with $u_*:=1/r_*$, $$\Delta:=\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu\,(E-V(r))}} =\int_0^{u_*}\frac{b\,\mathrm du}{\sqrt{1-\dfrac{\kappa}{E}u-b^2u^2}} =\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$

**(i) The two-label central model.** A model of class (i) is a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$ labels, fixed masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_0$, the collision-excluded configuration domain $$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$ for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and the force map presented through the time-independent **static central pair potential** $$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),\qquad u:J_0\to\mathbb R\ \text{of class }C^2,$$ so that $F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain (clauses (iii) and (iv) of [[post-cm02-interactions]]; $U$ is of class $C^2$ on the open $Q$ by [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). In the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of that postulate the model has $F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$: no external forces act on the labels of a model of class (i).

4. **(Reconstruction and bijection.)** The identities $x_1=X+\frac{m_2}{M}r$ and $x_2=X-\frac{m_1}{M}r$ hold on $J$. Conversely, if $X^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is affine with $(X^{\circ})''=0$ and $r^{\circ}:J\to\mathbb R^3$ is a $C^2$ curve with $\lvert r^{\circ}(t)\rvert\in J_0$ and $\mu(r^{\circ})''=-u'(\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert)r^{\circ}/\lvert r^{\circ}\rvert$ on $J$, then $$x_1^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}+\frac{m_2}{M}r^{\circ},\qquad x_2^{\circ}:=X^{\circ}-\frac{m_1}{M}r^{\circ}$$ define a motion $x^{\circ}:J\to Q$ of the model whose centre of mass is $X^{\circ}$ and whose relative coordinate is $r^{\circ}$. Consequently the assignment $x\mapsto(X,r)$ is a bijection from the motions of the model on $J$ onto the pairs (affine curve $X^{\circ}$ with $(X^{\circ})''=0$\!, central-force trajectory $r^{\circ}$ for $(\mu,u)$ with values in $J_0$) on $J$.

The curve $r$ is a **central-force trajectory for** $(\mu,U)$ when $$\mu\,r''(t)=-\frac{U'(|r(t)|)}{|r(t)|}\,r(t)\qquad(t\in I),$$ where $|x|:=\lVert x\rVert_2$ is the Euclidean norm ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]) and $U'$ is the derivative of $U$ on the open interval $J_0$. **Attached objects.** The **angular momentum vector** of such a trajectory is the curve $j:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $$j(t):=\mu\,r(t)\times r'(t),$$ with $\times$ the cross product of $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]]); its **energy** is the function $E:I\to\mathbb R$, $$E(t):=\tfrac12\mu\,\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2+U(|r(t)|);$$ and for every $J\ge0$ the **effective potential of momentum magnitude** $J$ is the function $U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J:J_0\to\mathbb R$, $$U^{\mathrm{eff}}_J(\rho):=U(\rho)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu\,\rho^2}.$$

Then: 1. the half-angle $$\Delta:=\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu\,(E-V(r))}}$$ is finite and positive, and $$\theta(\infty)-\theta(t_*)=\Delta=\theta(t_*)-\theta(-\infty),\qquad \theta(\infty)-\theta(-\infty)=2\Delta;$$ 2. $\displaystyle\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}n(\theta(t))$ exist and equal $v_+/|v_+|$ (as $t\to+\infty$) and $-v_-/|v_-|$ (as $t\to-\infty$); 3. consequently $$\frac{v_+}{|v_+|}=-R_{2\Delta}\Bigl(\frac{v_-}{|v_-|}\Bigr), \qquad \frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{|v_-|\,|v_+|}=-\cos 2\Delta=\cos(\pi-2\Delta);$$ in particular, if $0<\Delta<\pi/2$ then $\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi)$ is the (undirected) angle between the asymptotic velocity directions, and the signed velocity rotation is $-( \pi-2\Delta)$ in the orientation defined by $e_3$.

Let $\mu>0$, $\kappa>0$, $E>0$ and $J>0$, write $b:=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}>0$ for the asymptotic impact distance of [[thm-cm-coulomb-scattering]], and define the **deflection map** $$\theta_{\rm def}:(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi),\qquad \theta_{\rm def}(b):=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$ Then: 1. $\theta_{\rm def}$ is $C^1$ and strictly decreasing, with $\theta_{\rm def}(b)\to\pi$ as $b\downarrow0$ and $\theta_{\rm def}(b)\to0$ as $b\to\infty$; it is a $C^1$ bijection $(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi)$ with inverse $$b(\theta)=\frac{\kappa}{2E}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}\qquad(0<\theta<\pi).$$ 2. For every interval $(\theta_1,\theta_2)\subseteq(0,\pi)$ the pair $(\theta,b)$ is a deflection branch with cross-section density $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta) =b(\theta)\Bigl|\frac{\mathrm db}{\mathrm d\theta}(\theta)\Bigr|\frac{1}{\sin\theta} =\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2\csc^4\frac{\theta}{2},$$ finite and positive on $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$; and the pushforward of the incident flux measure under the branch is described by [[thm-cm-differential-cross-section-density]]. 3. For every $\theta_0\in(0,\pi)$ the truncated total cross-section $$\int_0^{\theta_0}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2 \csc^4\frac{\theta}{2}\,\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi\,\mathrm d\theta=+\infty,$$ while for $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ the integral over $(\theta_1,\theta_2)\times(0,2\pi)$ is finite; in this sense the total cross-section of the ideal Coulomb model diverges at forward angles and every finite angular acceptance cuts it off.

**Deflection branch.** A **deflection branch** is an interval $(a_1,a_2)\subseteq(0,\infty)$ with at least two points together with a function $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ that is of class $C^1$ and satisfies $\theta'(b)\ne0$ for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$. Such a $\theta$ is strictly monotone and its image is an interval with endpoints $\theta_1<\theta_2$ ([[def-interval]]); its inverse $b:(\theta_1,\theta_2)\to(a_1,a_2)$ is differentiable with $b'(\theta)=1/\theta'(b(\theta))$, by the derivative-of-an-inverse theorem [[thm-derivative-of-an-inverse]] applied to the continuous injective $\theta$ (every point of $(a_1,a_2)$ is a limit point of it, [[def-limit-point-r]], [[def-derivative]]). **Cross-section density.** The **cross-section density of the branch** is the function $$\frac{d\sigma}{d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|} \qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2).$$

**(i) The differential cross-section of a branch.** Let a central scattering model be given, let $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ be a **deflection branch** in the sense of [[def-cm-scattering-data]] — an interval $(a_1,a_2)$ of impact parameters with $\theta$ of class $C^1$ and $\theta'(b)\ne0$ — and suppose the branch **records the deflection** of the model: for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$ the scattering motion of the model with impact parameter $b$, energy $E$ and angular momentum $J$ has scattering angle $\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\theta(b)$. Write $(a_1,a_2)\ni b\mapsto\theta\in(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ for this bijection and $b(\theta):=\theta^{-1}(\theta)$ for its inverse ([[def-cm-scattering-data]]). The **differential cross-section of the branch** is the function $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|}\qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2),$$ the cross-section density of [[def-cm-scattering-data]].

By [[lem-tangent-principal-branch-is-bijective]], tangent restricts to a continuous strictly increasing bijection $$\tan:(-\pi/2,\pi/2)\longrightarrow\mathbb R.$$ Its inverse is the **principal inverse tangent** $$\arctan:\mathbb R\longrightarrow(-\pi/2,\pi/2).$$ Thus $\tan(\arctan y)=y$ for every real $y$, while $\arctan(\tan x)=x$ precisely for $x$ in the displayed principal interval. The inverse is continuous and strictly increasing by [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

Define $$	an x:= rac{\sin x}{\cos x}\quad(x
e\pi/2+m\pi),\qquad\cot x:= rac{\cos x}{\sin x}\quad(x
e m\pi),$$ $$\sec x:= rac1{\cos x}\quad(x

On their natural domains, $$(\tan x)'=\sec^2x,\qquad(\cot x)'=-\csc^2x,\qquad(\sec x)'=\sec x\tan x,\qquad(\csc x)'=-\csc x\cot x.$$ Tangent and cotangent have least positive period $\pi$; secant and cosecant have least positive period $2\pi$.

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with $g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite $f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable ([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$ at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Then $f$ is **continuous at $c$** when $$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ |f(x) - f(c)| < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$ with $\varepsilon$ and $\delta$ ranging over the **positive reals**. In the language of neighbourhoods: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real $\delta > 0$ with $$f\bigl(A \cap N_{\delta}(c)\bigr) \;\subseteq\; N_{\varepsilon}\bigl(f(c)\bigr).$$ $f$ is **continuous on $A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$ this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then: 1. **Nonnegativity.** If $f(x) \ge 0$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then $\int_a^b f \ge 0$. 2. **Monotonicity.** If $f(x) \le g(x)$ for every $x \in [a,b]$ then $$\int_a^b f \;\le\; \int_a^b g .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$: | | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms | |---|---|---|---| | $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ | | $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ | | $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ | | $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ | | | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is **closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$, $[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$.

derivations.claim: Clause 1: [L1] gives that $V$ is strictly decreasing from $+\infty$ to $0$ and that the unique solution $r_*$ of $V=E$ is simple with $V(r)<E$ for $r>r_*$; strict decrease also gives $V(r)>E$ for $0<r<r_*$. This is clause 1.

Clause 2, motion and asymptotics: by [L2] the relative coordinate is a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ with the attached data, so the trajectory hypotheses of [L1] hold; [L1] then gives the unique extension to all of $\mathbb R$ with no collision, the monotone branches with unique apsis, and the existence of $v_\pm$ with $|v_\pm|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$ and asymptotic perpendicular distance $b=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}$ on both branches. The extension is the relative coordinate of a motion of the model on all of $\mathbb R$ by [L2], since $|\bar r(t)|\in(0,\infty)$ keeps the configuration admissible and the affine centre-of-mass extension is defined on all of $\mathbb R$. Because $u\not\equiv0$ on any outer region, no exact free tail is asserted; this is clause 2.

Clause 3: [L1] gives $\Delta=\pi/2-\arctan(\kappa/(2Eb))$ with $\alpha=\kappa/(2Eb)>0$, so $\arctan\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$ and $\Delta\in(0,\pi/2)$; [L3] then gives the scattering angle $\theta_{\mathrm s}=\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi)$ and the signed rotation $2\Delta-\pi$; substituting the arctangent expression gives $\theta_{\mathrm s}=2\arctan(\kappa/(2Eb))$. [L3] further gives that $\theta_{\mathrm{def}}$ is $C^1$ and strictly decreasing with image $(0,\pi)$ and the stated inverse, and $\theta_{\mathrm{def}}'(b)=2\cdot\frac{1}{1+(\kappa/(2Eb))^2}\cdot(-\frac{\kappa}{2Eb^2})<0$, so $\theta_{\mathrm{def}}'\ne0$ everywhere and the single branch covers $(0,\infty)$. Since every $b>0$ gives $0<\Delta<\pi/2$, the branch never wraps. This is clause 3.

Clause 4, density: the cross-section density of the branch is $b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|/\sin\theta$ by [L3], and substituting $b'(\theta)=-(\kappa/4E)\csc^2(\theta/2)$ and $b(\theta)=(\kappa/2E)\cot(\theta/2)$ and using $\sin\theta=2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)$ and $\csc^2=1+\cot^2$ gives $(\kappa/(4E))^2\csc^4(\theta/2)$, finite and positive for $0<\theta<\pi$; this is the displayed density.

Clause 4, band computation: put $F(\theta):=\pi b(\theta)^2$. By [L4] and the chain rule, $F'(\theta)=2\pi b(\theta)b'(\theta) =2\pi\cdot\frac{\kappa}{2E}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}\cdot\bigl(-\frac{\kappa}{4E}\csc^2\frac{\theta}{2}\bigr) =-\frac{\kappa^2}{4E^2}\,\frac{\cos(\theta/2)}{\sin^3(\theta/2)}$, while the solid-angle integrand is $\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta)\,2\pi\sin\theta =\bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\bigr)^2\csc^4\frac{\theta}{2}\cdot 4\pi\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\cos\frac{\theta}{2} =\frac{\kappa^2}{4E^2}\frac{\cos(\theta/2)}{\sin^3(\theta/2)}=-F'(\theta)$, using $\sin\theta=2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)$. Hence by the fundamental theorem [L5], for $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ $$\sigma\bigl((\theta_1,\theta_2)\bigr)=\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta)\,2\pi\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta =-\bigl(F(\theta_2)-F(\theta_1)\bigr)=\pi\bigl(b(\theta_1)^2-b(\theta_2)^2\bigr),$$ finite because $b$ is continuous on $[\theta_1,\theta_2]$. Since the integrand is nonnegative, the truncated integral over $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ increases as $\theta_2\uparrow\pi$ and tends to $\pi b(\theta_1)^2$ because $b(\theta_2)^2\to0$; this gives the band value. The divergence of the truncated integral over $(0,\theta_0)$ is the corresponding clause of [L3]. This is clause 4.

Clause 5: the statement records only the mechanical model's parameter $\kappa$, its conditional prediction and the explicit exclusions; no identification, measurement or additional model is used in steps 1.1-5.1, each of which cites only model data and the cited mathematical and physical suppliers. This completes the proof.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ($\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, [[def-countable-choice]]), inherited from the jump lemma below.
Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $t_*\in I$, let $m_1,m_2>0$, and let $x_1,x_2:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous on $I$ and twice continuously differentiable on each of the two open intervals $I\cap(-\infty,t_*)$ and $I\cap(t_*,\infty)$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]). Assume the one-sided limits
$$v_i^-:=\lim_{t\uparrow t_*}x_i'(t),\qquad v_i^+:=\lim_{t\downarrow t_*}x_i'(t)\qquad(i=1,2)$$
exist in $\mathbb R^3$, and write $p_i:=m_ix_i'$ on $I\setminus\{t_*\}$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]). Let $F_1,F_2:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous and let $J\in\mathbb R^3$. The **isolated reciprocal impulse model** at $t_*$ consists of the two requirements:

1. regular dynamics off the impulse: $m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t)$ for every $t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}$ and $i=1,2$;
2. impulse pairing: for every $\Phi\in C_c^\infty(I;\mathbb R^3)$ — meaning every map whose three components lie in $C_c^\infty(I)$ ([[def-test-function-space-d-of-an-open-set]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]) — $$-\int_I\langle p_1(t),\Phi'(t)\rangle\,d\lambda(t)=\int_I\langle F_1(t),\Phi(t)\rangle\,d\lambda(t)+\langle J,\Phi(t_*)\rangle,$$ $$-\int_I\langle p_2(t),\Phi'(t)\rangle\,d\lambda(t)=\int_I\langle F_2(t),\Phi(t)\rangle\,d\lambda(t)-\langle J,\Phi(t_*)\rangle,$$ with integrals against Lebesgue measure $\lambda$ and the Euclidean inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]); the value of $p_i$ at $t_*$ is irrelevant.

Under this model, with $M:=m_1+m_2$ and $\mu:=m_1m_2/M$:

**a.** $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=J$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=-J$; consequently the total momentum is continuous across the impulse, $p_1(t_*^+)+p_2(t_*^+)=p_1(t_*^-)+p_2(t_*^-)$.

**b.** Let $e\in[0,1]$ satisfy the **restitution law** $v_2^+-v_1^+=-e(v_2^--v_1^-)$. Then the post-impulse velocities are uniquely determined: with $V:=\frac{m_1v_1^-+m_2v_2^-}{M}=\frac{m_1v_1^++m_2v_2^+}{M}$, $$v_1^+=V+\frac{m_2}{M}e\,(v_2^--v_1^-),\qquad v_2^+=V-\frac{m_1}{M}e\,(v_2^--v_1^-).$$

**c.** The kinetic-energy change across the impulse is $$\Delta K:=\frac{m_1\lVert v_1^+\rVert_2^2+m_2\lVert v_2^+\rVert_2^2}{2}-\frac{m_1\lVert v_1^-\rVert_2^2+m_2\lVert v_2^-\rVert_2^2}{2}=-\frac{1-e^2}{2}\,\mu\,\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2\le0;$$ in particular $\Delta K=0$ for $e=1$ and $\Delta K=-\frac12\mu\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2$ for $e=0$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and let $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be maps. Suppose the two **material balance identities**

$$m'(t)=r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t),\qquad (mv)'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)$$

hold for every $t\in I$, where $mv$ denotes the pointwise scalar multiple. Then

$$m(t)v'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in I).$$

In particular, if $F\equiv0$, $r_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv0$ and $r_{\mathrm{out}}\equiv r$ for a constant $r\ge0$, then $mv'=-r(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$: the acceleration is governed by the momentum carried away per unit time relative to the body, not by $(mv)'=0$.

The two balance identities are the **adopted content of the material momentum accounting** — the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,dt$ of matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,dt$ with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$". They are not derived here from any closed-system law; the deduction below is their product-rule consequence.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about
forces and motion, in the spacetime, frames and worldlines of
[[post-cm01-spacetime]], [[post-cm01-frames]] and [[post-cm01-worldlines]].

**(i) Setting and configuration domain.** A model of the framework has
$N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed positive masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]], clause (v)) and a configuration domain $Q$ in one
fixed inertial frame, in the unconstrained branch of
[[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a): $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ is open,
possibly with the collision set $\Delta$ removed when the force law of the
model is singular at coincident positions. The constrained branch of that
definition, with its reaction forces, is **not** covered by this postulate; the
dynamics of constrained systems is a separate development with its own
assumptions. A **state** of the model is a pair $z=(x,v)\in Q\times\mathbb
R^{3N}$ of positions and coordinate velocities of the labels in the chosen
frame ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]).

**(ii) Time window.** A model carries a nondegenerate open interval
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$, its **time window**, read in seconds
([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(iii) Force map and standing regularity.** A **force map** on this data is a
map

$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N},\qquad (t,x,v)\longmapsto F(t,x,v)=\bigl(F_{1}(t,x,v),\dots,F_{N}(t,x,v)\bigr),$$

with components of dimension $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, read in newtons
([[def-cm01-units]]). The standing hypotheses of this branch, which every
force map of a model is required to satisfy, are:

1. **Continuity.** $F$ is continuous on its domain
   $D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
2. **State-local Lipschitz regularity, locally uniform in time.** $F$ is
   locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z=(x,v)$, locally uniformly in
   time, in the sense of [[def-locally-lipschitz-in-the-state-variable]]: every
   compact cylinder $C\subseteq D$ carries a finite $L\ge0$ with
   $\lVert F(t,z)-F(t,z')\rVert_{2}\le L\lVert z-z'\rVert_{2}$ whenever
   $(t,z),(t,z')\in C$ share their time coordinate.

A map that fails clause 1 or clause 2 is **not** a force map of this branch,
whatever its other merits. When a later statement differentiates the force map
(for instance in a linearization or a smooth-dependence claim), it adds the
required differentiability hypothesis of the state variable explicitly; clause
2 alone licenses only the existence, uniqueness and continuation statements
proved on this page.

**(iv) Equation of motion.** Adopt: the motion of the labels of a model with
force map $F$ in an inertial frame is governed by

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N),$$

imposed along families of $C^{2}$ coordinate curves of the labels
$x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):J\to Q$, where $J\subseteq I_{0}$ is an interval with
nonempty interior and the derivatives are those of
[[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]. The precise notion of a motion of the
model, its associated first-order system and its maximal motions is
[[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. The force map is **primitive data** of the model:
the equations above are the model's law, not an operational definition of $F$
from a measured acceleration, and $F$ is not an extra observable measured
independently of the motion. The mass $m_{i}$ in (iv) is the fixed inertial
mass of clause (v) of [[post-cm01-worldlines]]; no other mass occurs in this
clause.

**(v) Additive composition of force contributions.** When a model presents its
force map as composed of contributions, the composition is the pointwise sum:
for force maps $F^{(1)},\dots,F^{(k)}$ on a common domain satisfying (iii),

$$F(t,z)=\sum_{a=1}^{k}F^{(a)}(t,z),$$

and the sum again satisfies (iii), because a finite sum of continuous maps is
continuous and a finite sum of maps that are locally Lipschitz in the state
variable is locally Lipschitz with a locally uniform constant. This
**superposition of forces** is an adopted modelling rule, not a theorem about
nature: it says how the model's total force is composed from the contributions
it declares. Two decompositions with the same sum define the same force map
and the same model; the framework does not measure an individual contribution
in isolation, and no observation of motions alone determines a decomposition.
Nor does (v) assert that sums of motions are motions: if $F$ is not affine in
the state, the sum of two solutions of (iv) generally does not satisfy (iv),
and superposing solutions is a separate question from superposing forces.

**(vi) Description in another inertial frame.** Let $F_{*}=\bigl(o',u',
(e_{1}',e_{2}',e_{3}')\bigr)$ be a second inertial frame related to the frame
of (i) by the Galilean transformation

$$t'=t+b,\qquad x'=Rx+vt+a_{0}$$

with $b\in\mathbb R$, $a_{0},v\in\mathbb R^{3}$ and $R\in SO(3)$
([[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]] clause 1;
[[def-cm-special-orthogonal-group]]). If $x:J\to Q$ is a family of motions of
the labels in the first frame and $\eta(t'):=R\,x(t'-b)+v\,(t'-b)+a_{0}$ is
the description of the same worldlines in the second frame, then by clause 2
of that theorem $\eta$ is of class $C^{2}$ on $J+b$ and
$\eta_{i}''(t')=R\,\ddot x_{i}(t'-b)$, so along the motion (iv) becomes

$$m_{i}\,\eta_{i}''(t')=\bigl(R\,F\bigl(t'-b,\ x(t'-b),\ \dot x(t'-b)\bigr)\bigr)_{i}.$$

Adopt: the same interaction, read in the second frame, is represented on the
transferred data by the map

$$F_{*}(t',y,w):=R\,F\Bigl(t'-b,\ R^{\mathsf T}\bigl(y-v(t'-b)-a_{0}\bigr),\ R^{\mathsf T}(w-v)\Bigr),$$

whose domain is the image of $D$ under the affine bijection
$(t',y,w)\mapsto\bigl(t'-b,\,R^{\mathsf T}(y-v(t'-b)-a_{0}),\,R^{\mathsf T}(w-v)\bigr)$;
that domain is open, and $F_{*}$ is continuous and locally Lipschitz in its
state variable because $F$ is and the transfer is an affine bijection with
bounded inverse on compacta. The framework formulates the equation of motion
in every inertial frame; a rule that does not transform by this law is a
description tied to the frame in which it was written, and the framework
attaches no kinematic covariance to it. When $Q=\mathbb R^{3N}$ — the case of
the models of the companion page — the transferred domain is again a product
$I_{0}'\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N}$ with $I_{0}'=I_{0}+b$, and
$F_{*}$ is a force map in the sense of (iii); for a bounded $Q$ the
transferred admissible position set may depend on $t'$, and the equation is
then read on that transferred set.

**(vii) What this branch excludes.** Impulsive forcing (a finite momentum
transfer at an instant is not a force map); Coulomb sliding friction, whose
expression contains the factor $v/\lvert v\rvert$ and is undefined at $v=0$;
static friction, which requires an inequality or a set-valued reaction model;
stochastic forcing; and forces that exist only as distributions. Each of these
requires its own stated model and solution notion, and none is covered by
(iii)–(iv). A singular force law is admissible on a configuration domain with
the singular configurations removed — for instance an inverse-square law on
the collision-excluded $Q$ of clause (i) — and what the removal of those
configurations implies for existence in time is stated by the continuation
theorem of this page.

**(viii) Status.** Clause (iii) states the hypotheses under which the theorems
of this page are proved; clause (iv) is the adopted law of motion; clauses (v)
and (vi) are the adopted composition and frame rules. Nothing here is deduced
from experiment, from a symmetry principle or from the uniqueness theory of
differential equations, and nothing here asserts that any physical
interaction is exactly of this form: the theorems of this page are conditional
consequences of the adopted model. The empirical significance of a concrete
model lies in fully specified model parameters and reported observations
compared with its predictions, and this postulate supplies neither.

Let a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] be given: time window
$I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb R$ nondegenerate and open, configuration domain
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ open ([[def-cm01-configuration]] clause (a)),
fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), and a
force map $F$ with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz
hypotheses of clause (iii) of that postulate.

**(a) State domain and inverse-mass operator.** The **state domain** of the
model is

$$D:=I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},$$

an open subset of $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{6N}$; a point $(t,x,v)\in D$ is a
time together with the **state** $z=(x,v)$ of positions $x\in Q$ and coordinate
velocities $v\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ of the labels ([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]],
[[def-cm01-units]]). The **inverse-mass operator** is the linear map

$$\mathsf M^{-1}:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathsf M^{-1}(u_{1},\dots,u_{N}):=\Bigl(\frac{u_{1}}{m_{1}},\dots,\frac{u_{N}}{m_{N}}\Bigr),$$

the inverse of the mass operator $\mathsf M$ of clause (d) of
[[def-cm01-configuration]].

**(b) Associated first-order system.** The **associated first-order field** of
the model is

$$\mathcal F:D\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \mathcal F(t,x,v):=\Bigl(v,\ \mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)\Bigr),$$

and the **associated first-order system** is $z'=\mathcal F(t,z)$ on the open
domain $D$, in the sense of
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]; here
$z=(x,v)\in\mathbb R^{6N}$. The map $\mathcal F$ satisfies the
Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses of
[[thm-picard-lindelof-local-existence-and-uniqueness]]: it is continuous on
$D$, and it is locally Lipschitz in the state variable $z$ locally uniformly
in time, because its first component $z\mapsto v$ is linear and its second is
the composition of the force map $F$ — which is locally Lipschitz in $(x,v)$
locally uniformly in time by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iii) —
with the linear map $\mathsf M^{-1}$.

**(c) Motions.** Let $J\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty
interior, endpoints read with one-sided derivatives as in
[[def-first-order-ode-initial-value-problem-and-solution]]. A **motion** of
the model on $J$ is a curve $x:J\to Q$ of class $C^{2}$ such that
$t\in I_{0}$ for every $t\in J$ and

$$m_{i}\,\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),\dot x(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J).$$

Equivalently: the state curve $z=(x,\dot x):J\to D$ is a solution of the
associated first-order system on $J$. Indeed, if $x$ is a motion then
$z=(x,x')$ is $C^{1}$ with
$z'=(x',x'')=(x',\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,x'))=\mathcal F(t,z)$ and $z(t)\in D$;
conversely, if $z=(x,v)$ is a solution with $z(t)\in D$ for all $t$, then
$x'=v$ and $v'=\mathsf M^{-1}F(t,x,v)$, so $v$ is $C^{1}$, $x$ is $C^{2}$, and
multiplying the second equation by the masses returns the displayed
second-order equation. Motions of the labels of the model are exactly these
curves by [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] clause (iv).

**(d) Initial data and maximal motion.** An **initial datum** of the model is
a triple $(t_{0},x_{0},v_{0})$ with $t_{0}\in I_{0}$, $x_{0}\in Q$ and
$v_{0}\in(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; write $z_{0}:=(x_{0},v_{0})$. A **maximal
motion** with this datum is a motion $x:J_{\max}\to Q$ with $x(t_{0})=x_{0}$
and $\dot x(t_{0})=v_{0}$ that has no extension to a motion of the model on a
strictly larger interval. By the Picard–Lindelöf hypotheses verified in (b)
and the maximal-solution theorem
[[thm-existence-and-uniqueness-of-a-maximal-ode-solution]] (with
[[def-maximal-ode-solution]]): every initial datum has exactly one maximal
motion, its **maximal interval** $J_{\max}$ is an open interval containing
$t_{0}$ and contained in $I_{0}$, and every motion with the same datum is the
restriction of the maximal one. The restriction statement transfers from the
associated first-order system to motions through the equivalence in (c).

**(e) Newtonian flow.** The **Newtonian flow** of the model is the map

$$\Phi:\Omega\longrightarrow Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\qquad \Omega:=\bigl\{(t,t_{0},z_{0}):t_{0}\in I_{0},\ z_{0}\in Q\times\mathbb R^{3N},\ t\in J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})\bigr\},$$

defined by $\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0}):=z(t)$, where $t\mapsto z(t)=(x(t),\dot x(t))$
is the state curve of the maximal motion with datum $(t_{0},z_{0})$. By (d) the
assignment is well defined: the maximal motion is unique, so $\Phi$ is a
function on $\Omega$ and not merely a relation. For fixed $t_{0}$ and $z_{0}$
the curve $t\mapsto\Phi(t;t_{0},z_{0})$ is defined exactly on the maximal
interval $J_{\max}(t_{0},z_{0})$.

Fix a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$
particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb
R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with its collision
set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an
interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). All sums below range over
$i=1,\dots,N$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $u\times v$, $\langle u,v\rangle$
and $\lVert u\rVert_{2}$ are the cross product, the Euclidean inner product and
the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(a) Curve families and motions.** A **curve family** of the model is a map
$x:J\to Q$, $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$, of class $C^{2}$ on $J$
([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]); its **coordinate velocities** are
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$ on $J$, written $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{N}):J\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
A curve family is a **motion** of the model when
$$m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J),$$
the notion of clause (c) of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Every quantity of
this definition is defined for an arbitrary curve family; the balance theorems
of this page state which of their properties use the equations of motion.
Along a curve family the force map is evaluated at $(t,x(t),w(t))\in
I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; when the model invokes the
external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the maps $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $F_{ij}$ are evaluated at their declared
arguments on the motion's state graph, where the presentation is an identity
for $F_{i}$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define
$$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$
Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$
the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$.
The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]). Since $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$, each $p_{i}$ is $C^{1}$ and
each of $P$, $X$, $\rho_{i}$ is differentiable, as a finite sum of
differentiable curves ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); write
$$V:=X'$$
for the **centre-of-mass velocity**. The algebraic identities
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0$, $P=MV$ and the splitting of the kinetic sum
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}$ are proved in the kinetic-splitting
theorem of this page; they are not part of this definition.

**(c) Angular momentum, torque, internal torque sum.** Let a **reference

moments are taken, allowed to move (a constant map $o\equiv o_{0}$ is the
fixed-origin case). Define the **angular momentum about $o$** and the **total
torque about $o$** by
$$J_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times p_{i}(t),\qquad T_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),$$
with dimensions $[J_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{2}\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and
$[T_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m$). When the
model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]], define in addition the **external torque** and the
**internal torque sum**
$$T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr),\qquad I(t):=\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)\bigr)\times F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr).$$
The sum $I$ does not involve $o$; it is defined whenever the pair
presentation is declared. The identity $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$ uses the
antisymmetry $F_{ji}=-F_{ij}$ of clause (ii)1 of that postulate to reindex the
ordered pairs and is proved as step 1.1 of the angular-momentum balance of
this page.

**(d) Kinetic energy, power, work.** Define the **kinetic energy** and the
**power of the total force** along the curve family by
$$K(t):=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}(t)\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad \mathcal P(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl\langle F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),\,w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle,$$
of dimensions $[K]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules) and
$[\mathcal P]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-3}$ (read in watts), and for
$t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$ the **work of the total force** over $[t_{0},t_{1}]$ by
$$W([t_{0},t_{1}]):=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt,$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules); $\mathcal P$ is
continuous on $J$ because $F$, $x$ and $w$ are continuous, so the Riemann
integral exists ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], see the page
`the-riemann-integral`). The **potential energy** is not defined by this item:
it belongs to the potential branch of the model and is defined in the
potential-and-mechanical-energy item of this page.

**(e) Frame and reference-point dependence.** The quantities $p_{i}$, $P$,
$X$, $\rho_{i}$, $V$, $K$, $\mathcal P$ and $W$ are read in the one inertial
frame fixed above, and $J_{o}$, $T_{o}$, $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$, $I$ are read
about the reference curve $o$ in that frame. They are not invariant under a
change of frame or reference point: their transformation laws under a change
of inertial frame are stated and proved in the frame-transformation item of
this page, and every conservation statement involving them names the frame
and the reference point in which it is made.

**(f) Status.** This item is a definition: it introduces symbols, their
domains, regularity, dimensions and frame dependence from the model's data.
It adopts no force law beyond the force branch already fixed, asserts no
balance of any of these quantities and records no measured value.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and vector-valued functions, their
