### The derivative

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $c \in A$ be
a **limit point of $A$** ([[def-limit-point-r]]). The **difference quotient of
$f$ at $c$** is the vector-valued function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) \;:=\; \frac{1}{x - c}\,\bigl(f(x) - f(c)\bigr),$$

the scalar multiple being that of the vector space $\mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-function-space]]); the division is legitimate because $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$. As in [[def-derivative]], $c$ is a limit point of
$A \setminus \{c\}$ as well, since a punctured neighbourhood of $c$ omits $c$.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ exists in
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$, and then the **derivative** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x\to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;\in\; \mathbb{R}^{m}.$$

**The notation denotes a single vector.** At most one $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$
satisfies the limit condition, as proved in
[[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]; this is the vector-valued
form of the obligation [[lem-function-limit-unique]] discharges for real-valued
functions and [[lem-metric-limits-unique]] for sequences.

**The intrinsic form is the definition; the componentwise form is a theorem.**
For $i < m$ the $i$-th component of $q_{f,c}(x)$ is
$\bigl(f_i(x)-f_i(c)\bigr)/(x-c)$, which is the real difference quotient of
$f_i$ at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]). So by
[[thm-componentwise-limits-and-continuity]] clause 2:

> $f$ is differentiable at $c$ **if and only if** every $f_i$ is differentiable
> at $c$, and then $f'(c)_i = f_i'(c)$ for every $i<m$.

Nothing below reverses this order of presentation: the intrinsic limit is what is
defined, and the coordinates are read off it.

**Algebra of derivatives.** If $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are differentiable at
$c$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $f + g$ and $\lambda f$ are differentiable
at $c$ with $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c)+g'(c)$ and $(\lambda f)'(c) = \lambda f'(c)$: read
componentwise through the displayed equivalence, these are clauses 1 and 2 of the
published [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]].

### The integral

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$
([[def-interval]]). $f$ is **integrable on $[a,b]$** when every component
$f_i : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Darboux
integrable in the sense of [[def-darboux-integral]], and then

$$\int_a^b f \;:=\; \text{the function } m \to \mathbb{R} \text{ sending } i \mapsto \int_a^b f_i .$$

**That really is an element of $\mathbb{R}^{m}$.** In this library
$\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is the set of functions $m \to \mathbb{R}$
([[def-function-space]]), not a set of tuples, so the displayed assignment is
literally an element of it; each value $\int_a^b f_i$ is a single real by
[[def-darboux-integral]]. In the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]) the same object is
$\int_a^b f = \sum_{i<m}\bigl(\int_a^b f_i\bigr)e_i$.

**Oriented limits.** Following [[def-oriented-integral]] componentwise, set

$$\int_a^a f \;:=\; 0 \in \mathbb{R}^{m}, \qquad \int_b^a f \;:=\; -\int_a^b f \quad (a < b),$$

so that $\int_u^v f = -\int_v^u f$ for all $u,v$ in an interval on which $f$ is
integrable. The clauses do not overlap with the case $a<b$, so nothing has to be
checked for consistency, exactly as in [[def-oriented-integral]].

**Linearity.** If $f, g : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ are integrable and
$\lambda,\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ then $\lambda f + \mu g$ is integrable with

$$\int_a^b (\lambda f + \mu g) \;=\; \lambda\int_a^b f + \mu\int_a^b g ,$$

since each side has $i$-th coordinate $\int_a^b(\lambda f_i + \mu g_i)$ and
$\lambda\int_a^b f_i + \mu\int_a^b g_i$ respectively, and those agree by
[[thm-linearity-of-the-integral]].

**Restriction and splitting.** If $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ then it is
integrable on every nondegenerate closed subinterval $[c,d]$ with
$a\le c<d\le b$, and for $a<c<b$,
$\int_a^b f = \int_a^c f + \int_c^b f$; both are the componentwise readings of
[[lem-integrability-on-a-subinterval]] and
[[thm-additivity-over-subintervals]], applied to each $f_i$ and reassembled
coordinate by coordinate.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $N\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ and let $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable at every point of $I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Put $M:=\sum_{i}m_i>0$, $X:=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_ix_i$ and $\rho_i:=x_i-X$; all sums over $i$ range over $1,\dots,N$ (the index set $\{1,\dots,N\}$ of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are the Euclidean inner product and norm on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

1. $X$ and every $\rho_i$ are differentiable on $I$, with $X'=M^{-1}\sum_im_ix_i'$ and $\rho_i'=x_i'-X'$, and the identities $\sum_im_i\rho_i=0$ and $\sum_im_i\rho_i'=0$ hold on $I$;
2. for every $t\in I$, $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\sum_{i}m_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2;$$
3. if $N=2$, then with $r:=x_1-x_2$ and $\mu:=m_1m_2/M$ one has $\sum_im_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$ and hence $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$$ for every $t\in I$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Throughout, $m \in \mathbb{N}$ with $m \ge 1$, and $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ carries the
Euclidean norm $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]] and
[[def-p-norms-on-rn]], whose induced metric is the published $d_2$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]],
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). A function into $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ is called
**vector-valued**.

### Continuity

Let $(X, d_X)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]), let $A \subseteq X$
carry the restricted metric $d_A$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]), let
$f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ and let $a \in A$. Then $f$ is **continuous at $a$**
when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ d_X(x,a) < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ \lVert f(x) - f(a)\rVert_2 < \varepsilon\ \bigr],$$

with $\varepsilon, \delta$ ranging over the positive reals, and **continuous on
$A$** when it is continuous at every point of $A$.

**This is not a new notion, and that is the point of writing it down.** Since
$\lVert f(x)-f(a)\rVert_2 = d_2\bigl(f(x),f(a)\bigr)$ and $d_A$ is the
restriction of $d_X$, the displayed condition is **verbatim** the condition of
[[def-metric-continuity]] for the map of metric spaces
$f : (A,d_A) \to (\mathbb{R}^{m}, d_2)$. So every theorem about continuous maps
of metric spaces applies to vector-valued functions with no translation, and
this library has exactly one notion of continuity here. The same move was made
once before, between the $\mathbb{R}$-native and the metric notions, in
[[lem-real-and-metric-notions-agree]]; this item is that move one dimension up in
the codomain.

The two cases used below are $X = \mathbb{R}$ with $d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$
([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]) and $X = \mathbb{R}^{n}$ with $d_2$, for
$n \ge 1$.

### Limits, for a real domain

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$, let $c$ be a limit
point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) and let $L \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$. We say
$f(x)$ **tends to $L$ as $x$ tends to $c$**, and write
$\lim_{x\to c} f(x) = L$, when

$$(\forall \varepsilon > 0)\ (\exists \delta > 0)\ (\forall x \in A)\ \bigl[\ 0 < |x - c| < \delta \ \Longrightarrow\ \lVert f(x) - L\rVert_2 < \varepsilon\ \bigr].$$

This is the condition of [[def-function-limit]] with the absolute value in the
codomain replaced by $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$; as there, the puncture $0 < |x-c|$ is
what makes $c$ a point the function need not be defined at, and the hypothesis
that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is what stops the condition from being satisfied
vacuously.

**The notation denotes: at most one $L$ satisfies the condition.** Suppose $L$
and $L'$ both do and $L \ne L'$. Then $\varepsilon := \lVert L-L'\rVert_2 / 2 > 0$
by (N1) for $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]). Take $\delta$
and $\delta'$ for this $\varepsilon$ and put $\eta := \min\{\delta,\delta'\} > 0$.
Since $c$ is a limit point of $A$ there is $x \in A$ with $0 < |x-c| < \eta$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), and then

$$\lVert L - L'\rVert_2 \;\le\; \lVert L - f(x)\rVert_2 + \lVert f(x) - L'\rVert_2 \;<\; \varepsilon + \varepsilon \;=\; \lVert L-L'\rVert_2$$

by (N3) and (N2), which trichotomy forbids. So $L = L'$.

### Components

For $i < m$ define the $i$-th **coordinate projection**
$\pi_i : \mathbb{R}^{m} \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\pi_i(y) := y_i = y(i)$, and for
$f : A \to \mathbb{R}^{m}$ the $i$-th **component** $f_i := \pi_i \circ f$, a
real-valued function on $A$.

**Each $\pi_i$ is $1$-Lipschitz** ([[def-lipschitz-holder-contraction]]): for
$y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{m}$,

$$\bigl|\pi_i(y) - \pi_i(z)\bigr| \;=\; |y_i - z_i| \;\le\; \lVert y - z\rVert_2 \;=\; d_2(y,z),$$

the middle inequality being $|w_i| \le \lVert w\rVert_2$ at $w := y-z$
([[lem-every-norm-on-rn-is-continuous-for-the-euclidean-metric]] clause 3, or
directly because $w_i^{2}$ is one term of the sum $\sum_{k<m}w_k^{2}$). Written
in coordinates, $f(x)$ is the vector whose $i$-th coordinate is $f_i(x)$, and
$f(x) = \sum_{i<m} f_i(x)\,e_i$ in the standard basis
([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]).

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $U,V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open. A bijection $f:U\to V$ is a **$C^k$ diffeomorphism** when both $f$ and $f^{-1}$ are $C^k$. For $k\ge1$, a **local $C^k$ diffeomorphism at $a\in U$** is a restriction $f|_P:P\to Q$ between open neighbourhoods of $a$ and $f(a)$ that is a $C^k$ diffeomorphism. At $k=1$ this agrees with [[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]: continuous first partial derivatives give the required total derivative by [[thm-continuous-partial-derivatives-imply-total-differentiability]], while continuity of the total derivative gives continuity of its matrix entries and hence of the first partial derivatives.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework the following statements about particles and their motion, in the spacetime of [[post-cm01-spacetime]] and the frames of [[post-cm01-frames]].

**(i) Particle labels and worldlines.** A model of the framework has **particle
labels** $i=1,\dots,N$ for some $N\ge1$. To each label and each *inertial
frame* of the model — an adapted chart $(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ with
coordinates $(t,x)$ in the sense of [[post-cm01-frames]] — there is assigned a
**worldline** $\gamma_{i}:I\to A$ described in that frame, where
$I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval — that is, an interval
of the form $(a,b)$ with $-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points —
the curve $\gamma_{i}$ is of class $C^{2}$ in the adapted coordinates of the frame,
and the **parameter condition**

$$\tau\bigl(\gamma_{i}(t)-o\bigr)=t\qquad(t\in I)$$

holds: the curve parameter is the elapsed time from the origin of the frame, so
in the frame's coordinates $\gamma_{i}(t)=(t,x_{i}(t))$ with
$x_{i}:I\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{2}$. The parameter condition replaces
the causal conditions of relativistic kinematics: no timelike condition on the
velocity and no upper bound on its Euclidean norm is imposed, and the
parameter is not free up to reparametrization.

**(ii) Description in another frame.** The same motion described in a second
inertial frame is the curve obtained by the time reparametrization of the two
frames: if $(t',x')$ are the coordinates of the second frame and
$t'=t+b$ is the time component of the transformation between the two frames
([[post-cm01-frames]], [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]]),
then the description of the motion in the second frame is the curve
$\gamma_{i,b}(t'):=\gamma_{i}(t'-b)$, defined on $I+b$, and it again satisfies
the parameter condition $\tau(\gamma_{i,b}(t')-o')=t'$ with respect to the
second frame's origin $o'$. This is a consistency requirement of the model's
frame language; the accompanying spatial transformation of the coordinate
curve is the affine law of [[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]],
and its kinematic consequences are proved in [[pthm-cm01-galilean-kinematics]].

**(iii) Regularity is frame-independent.** The class of the worldline is
independent of the frame used to describe it: by the transformation law of
[[lem-cm-adapted-charts-and-galilean-transformations]], the coordinates of the
same event in two inertial frames differ by
$t'=t+b$, $x'=Rx+vt+a$ with constant $b,a,v$ and $R\in SO(3)$, so a coordinate
curve is twice continuously differentiable in one inertial frame exactly when
its reparametrized description is twice continuously differentiable in the
other. The assumptions of this postulate are therefore read in any one inertial
frame without loss.

**(iv) Velocity and acceleration.** In a fixed inertial frame the quantities
$w_{i}:=dx_{i}/dt$ and $a_{i}:=d^{2}x_{i}/dt^{2}$ are the **coordinate
velocity** and **coordinate acceleration** of the label, of dimensions
$\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $\ell\tau^{-2}$ by [[def-cm01-units]]; they are defined
precisely, and their transformation under a change of inertial frame is
recorded, in [[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]].

**(v) Fixed inertial mass.** Each particle label $i$ carries a **mass**
$m_{i}>0$, a primitive parameter of the model with dimension $\mu$
([[def-cm01-units]]). The mass is fixed: it is the same positive number at all
times, in all inertial frames and for every model in which the label occurs; it
is not a function of the time coordinate, of the position or of the velocity,
and no variable-mass model is a model of this clause. The mass enters the
dynamics only through its later appearance in the equation of motion; this
postulate attaches no dynamics to it. Distinct labels may carry distinct
masses, and the masses are model data, not measured values.

**(vi) Point-particle idealization.** The model retains of each label only its
position and its fixed mass, together with the label index: size, shape, spin,
deformation, temperature and internal degrees of freedom are omitted, and the
quantity $x_{i}(t)$ is the single point representing the label at time $t$. An
application of the model must state when this idealization is adequate for the
system at hand; for a body whose rotation, deformation or internal structure
matters for the question asked, the point-particle model is not adequate and a
richer model must be specified. The framework makes no claim that every
physical body is a point particle.

**(vii) Calibration caveat.** An apparatus calibration may *estimate* a mass
parameter of a concrete body under a stated measurement model, with its
assumptions, sampling and uncertainty; such an estimate neither defines the
mass parameter of a label nor verifies the equation of motion in which it
occurs, and it is not deduced from this postulate. No measured value of any
mass is asserted by this item.

Let $N\ge1$ particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$ be given as
in [[post-cm01-worldlines]], and fix one inertial frame of the model with
spatial coordinates $x_{i}\in\mathbb R^{3}$ for each label $i$. Identify the
space of all position tuples with $\mathbb R^{3N}=(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$ and
write its points as $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$; each component $x_{i}$ has
dimension $\ell$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(a) Unconstrained branch.** The **unconstrained configuration domain** is an
open set $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$, chosen as part of the model. A tuple
$x\in Q$ is an **admissible configuration**: an assignment of one position to
each label at one time. A **singular-force exclusion** is the removal of the
**collision set**

$$\Delta:=\Bigl\{x\in\mathbb R^{3N}:\ \text{there are }i\ne j\text{ with }x_{i}=x_{j}\Bigr\}$$

from the domain, which is done when the model's force law is not defined at
coincident positions: $\Delta$ is closed (it is the union of the finitely many
closed sets $\{x_{i}=x_{j}\}$, each the zero set of the continuous map
$x\mapsto x_{i}-x_{j}$), so $Q:=\mathbb R^{3N}\setminus\Delta$ is open and is a
legitimate configuration domain. Whether the exclusion is part of the model is
a modelling decision recorded with the force law; the framework itself only
requires $Q$ to be open and stated.

**(b) Holonomic constraint branch.** Let $O\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ be an open
**ambient set**, let $k\in\mathbb N$ with $1\le k\le3N-1$, and let

$$G=(G_{1},\dots,G_{k}):O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k}$$

be a smooth map, each component carrying a declared dimension and unit fixed
by the model (a component can always be rescaled by a nonzero constant without
changing its zero set, and the rescaling is part of the declaration). Assume:

1. **Nonempty level set:** $G^{-1}(0)\ne\varnothing$;
2. **Rank condition:** the differential $DG(x):\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{k}$
   is surjective, equivalently has rank $k$, at every $x\in G^{-1}(0)$.

Then $0$ is a regular value of $G$ in the sense of
[[def-regular-and-critical-points-and-values]], and the **constrained
configuration space** is $Q:=G^{-1}(0)$. By
[[thm-a-regular-level-set-is-an-embedded-submanifold]] — applied to the smooth
map $G$ from the open subset $O$ of $\mathbb R^{3N}$ to $\mathbb R^{k}$, whose
regular value $0$ has nonempty fibre — $Q$ is an embedded submanifold of
$\mathbb R^{3N}$ of dimension $3N-k$ ([[def-embedded-submanifold-and-slice-chart]]).
The **degrees of freedom** of this branch of the model is the number
$$\dim Q=3N-k.$$ In the sense of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]], $Q$ together with the inclusion $X:Q\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^{3N}$ is then a particle configuration, and the mass metric of that definition is available with the masses $m_{i}$; the configuration is constrained to $Q$ for all times in this branch.

**(c) Time-dependent holonomic constraints.** If the constraint map depends on
time,

$$G:\mathbb R\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^{k},\qquad (t,x)\longmapsto G(t,x),$$

with $G$ smooth and $D_{x}G(t_{0},x)$ of rank $k$ at every $x$ of the nonempty
set $G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$, then for each fixed $t_{0}\in\mathbb R$ the
**instantaneous configuration space** $Q_{t_{0}}:=G(t_{0},\cdot)^{-1}(0)$ is an
embedded submanifold of dimension $3N-k$ by the same theorem applied to
$G(t_{0},\cdot)$. The family $\{Q_{t_{0}}\}$ varies with $t_{0}$; a curve
$t\mapsto q(t)$ with $G(t,q(t))=0$ is not thereby a curve in one fixed
manifold, and the kinematic treatment of such constraints (velocities, the
reaction forces that maintain them and the distinction between rheonomic and
scleronomic constraints) belongs to the framework's constraint development and
is not part of this definition.

**(d) Mass operator.** In the ambient coordinates define the **mass operator**
$\mathsf M:\mathbb R^{3N}\to\mathbb R^{3N}$ by block multiplication,

$$\mathsf M(x_{1},\dots,x_{N}):=(m_{1}x_{1},\dots,m_{N}x_{N});$$

its matrix in the standard basis is block diagonal with blocks $m_{i}I_{3}$,
the **mass matrix** of [[def-cm-constrained-configuration-and-mass-metric]].
Its dimension is $\mu$: it multiplies positions of dimension $\ell$ by masses
of dimension $\mu$. On the constrained branch the mass metric restricts the
Euclidean inner product to $Q$ as in that item.

**(e) Velocity constraints are a different object.** A **velocity-map
constraint** of the model is a pair $(A,b)$ with
$A:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'}$ a smooth map of rows and
$b:\mathbb R\times O\to\mathbb R^{k'}$, imposing $A(t,x)\,\dot x+b(t,x)=0$ on
velocities. Such a constraint is called **nonholonomic** when its admissible
velocities are not the tangent spaces of position-constraint submanifolds. The
rank of $A(t,x)$ is a count of independent instantaneous velocity restrictions
and is not a dimension of a configuration manifold; no relation between that
rank and the number $\dim Q$ of clause (b) is asserted by this definition, and
no accessibility dimension is defined here. The framework's treatment of
nonholonomic models, and the distinction between their equations and those of
positional constraints, is developed separately.

Adopt, as this page's **impact and open-mass extensions** of the force
branch of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the following three model extensions. Each is an adopted model, not a
consequence of the smooth-force postulates; each applies only where a
statement explicitly invokes it.

**(i) The isolated reciprocal impulse model.** A two-label force model with
masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), time window $I_0$,
configuration domain $Q$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]) and continuous
external-plus-pair force maps $F_1,F_2$ is **run in the isolated reciprocal
impulse model at $t_*\in I_0$** when there is a motion
$x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ of the associated first-order system
([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]) such that:

1. $x_1,x_2$ are continuous on $I$ and twice continuously differentiable on
   each of $I\cap(-\infty,t_*)$ and $I\cap(t_*,\infty)$
   ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]],
   [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and
   $m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ for every $t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}$;
2. the one-sided limits
   $v_i^{\pm}:=\lim_{t\to t_*\pm}x_i'(t)$ exist in $\mathbb R^3$
   ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]);
3. there is a vector $J\in\mathbb R^3$, the **impulse**, with
   $$m_1\bigl(v_1^+-v_1^-\bigr)=J,\qquad m_2\bigl(v_2^+-v_2^-\bigr)=-J .$$

The two equations of clause 3 are the **reciprocal finite-jump form** of the
isolated impulse: the two labels receive equal and opposite momentum changes.
The model places no bound on the force maps across $t_*$; its distributional
rendering by test-function pairings is proved in
[[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]]. The dimension of the impulse
is $[J]=\mathsf M\ell\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

**(ii) The collinear restitution contact law.** A model run in the isolated
reciprocal impulse model at $t_*$ is **collinear** when there is a unit vector
$n\in\mathbb R^3$ (the **contact direction**) with $v_i^{\pm}\parallel n$ for
$i=1,2$ and $\langle v_2^--v_1^-,n\rangle<0$ (the labels approach along $n$).
For a collinear contact, adopt a **coefficient of restitution** $e\in[0,1]$ —
a dimensionless model datum of the pair and the contact — and the **restitution
law**
$$v_2^+-v_1^+=-e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$
For $e=1$ the contact is called **elastic**, for $e=0$ **perfectly inelastic**
and otherwise **semi-elastic**; the law is a constitutive assumption, not a
consequence of the impulse equations of clause (i), and $e$ is not derived
from the masses or the approach speed. The law is stated only for a single
collinear contact; simultaneous contacts, repeated contacts and tangential
(friction) impulses are outside the model.

**(iii) The open-body material accounting.** Adopt for a body whose mass,
velocity, external force and exchanged matter are described by maps
$m:I\to(0,\infty)$, $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$,
$r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and
$w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ (mass rates and *inertial*
velocities of the matter entering and leaving, measured in the same inertial
frame as $v$) the **material balance identities**
$$m'=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad (mv)'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}\,w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}\,w_{\mathrm{out}} .$$
They are the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathrm dt$ of
matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,\mathrm dt$
with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$", and they
are adopted rather than derived from a closed-system law. Their product-rule
consequence $mv'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$
is proved in [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]]; in particular the
closed-system law $(mv)'=F$ is recovered only when
$r_{\mathrm{in}}w_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$.
The model parameters $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}},w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}$
are model data with $[r_{\mathrm{in}}]=[r_{\mathrm{out}}]=\mathsf M\tau^{-1}$
and $[w_{\mathrm{in}}]=[w_{\mathrm{out}}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$.

derivations.claim: Clause 1: by [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (i) and [L1], $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=J$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=-J$; adding gives $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)+m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=0$, which is exactly $P(t_*^+)=P(t_*^-)$. This is clause 1.

Clause 2: let $x$ be a smooth-branch motion with continuous force maps along it. By [L3] the curves $x_i''=F_i/m_i$ are continuous, hence $x_i$ is $C^2$ and $p_i=m_ix_i'$ is $C^1$ on $I$; a $C^1$ function on an interval has equal one-sided limits at every interior point, so $p_i(t_*^+)=p_i(t_*^-)$ and therefore $J=0$. Thus the model of clause (i) with $J\ne0$ is outside this class, as asserted.

Clause 3: the collinear contact satisfies the hypotheses of [L1] on the relative velocity, so [L1] gives $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=J=-m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)$ and the displayed velocities with $V$ the centre-of-mass velocity; since $v_2^--v_1^-\parallel n$ and $J=\mu(1+e)(v_2^--v_1^-)$ is a scalar multiple of it, $J\parallel n$. The explicit identity $J=\mu(1+e)(v_2^--v_1^-)$ follows from the two jump equations and the restitution law: subtracting the second from the first, $v_2^+-v_1^+=(v_2^--v_1^-)-\frac{J}{\mu}$, which by the restitution law equals $-e(v_2^--v_1^-)$, so $J=\mu(1+e)(v_2^--v_1^-)$.

Clause 4: [L1] gives the kinetic-energy change $-\frac{1-e^2}{2}\mu\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2$, which is $\le0$ because $0\le e\le1$, and vanishes exactly when $e=1$ or $v_2^-=v_1^-$ (if $e<1$ and $v_2^-\ne v_1^-$ it is strictly negative). The identification statement is a statement of the scope of the model: the deficit is computed from the contact law, and no measured observable of another framework is introduced or equated with it. This is clause 4.

Clause 5: fix any real $J_n\le\mu d_n$ and put $v_1^+:=v_1^-+\frac{J_n}{m_1}n$, $v_2^+:=v_2^--\frac{J_n}{m_2}n$; then $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=J_nn$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=-J_nn$, so the reciprocal impulse equations of clause 1 hold with impulse $J=J_nn$, and adding the two equations shows that the total momentum is preserved. The relative velocity becomes $d^+=d^--\frac{J_n}{\mu}n$; hence $d^+\cdot n=d_n-\frac{J_n}{\mu}\ge0$ precisely for $J_n\le\mu d_n$, which is the stated admissibility (the contact separates or grazes). By the kinetic identity [L4], $\Delta K(J_n)=\frac{\mu}{2}\bigl(\lVert d^+\rVert_2^2-\lVert d^-\rVert_2^2\bigr) =\frac{\mu}{2}\bigl(-2\frac{J_n}{\mu}d_n+\frac{J_n^2}{\mu^2}\bigr) =-J_nd_n+\frac{J_n^2}{2\mu}$, a quadratic in $J_n$ with minimum $-\frac{\mu}{2}d_n^2$ at $J_n=\mu d_n$; the restitution law selects $J_n=\mu(1+e)d_n$, which lies in the admissible range because $1+e\ge1$ and $d_n<0$, and reproduces clause 3.

Clause 6: [L2] gives the derived law from the material balance identities, and the three special cases are its substitutions: (a) $r_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$ leaves $mv'=F$, while $(mv)'=m'v+mv'=F$ because $m'=0$; (b) $r_{\mathrm{in}}=0$, $r_{\mathrm{out}}=-m'$ gives $mv'=F-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)=F+r_{\mathrm{out}}(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})$; and $(mv)'=m'v+mv'=F+r_{\mathrm{out}}(v-w_{\mathrm{out}})+m'v=F-r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}+r_{\mathrm{out}}v-r_{\mathrm{out}}v=F-r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$, which equals $F$ exactly when $w_{\mathrm{out}}=v$ (or $r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$); (c) $r_{\mathrm{out}}=0$, $w_{\mathrm{in}}=0$ gives $mv'=F-r_{\mathrm{in}}v$, while $(mv)'=m'v+mv'=r_{\mathrm{in}}v+F-r_{\mathrm{in}}v=F$. This is clause 6.

boundaries.evidence: The interval $I$ is nonempty with $t_*\in I$ and the label set $\{1,2\}$ is nonempty; step 1.2 uses the motion on $I$.
The perfectly inelastic value $e=0$ is included; step 1.3 handles every $e\in[0,1]$ and step 1.4 records that the energy change vanishes exactly at $e=1$ or $v_2^-=v_1^-$.
One impulse vector $J$ and one contact direction $n$; step 1.1 pairs the two momentum changes through the single $J$.
The collinear contact is the degenerate one-dimensional geometry solved in steps 1.3-1.5, and the grazing endpoint $J_n=\mu d_n$ lies in the admissible range of step 1.5.
The one-sided limits at $t_*$ and the endpoint $e=1$ of $[0,1]$ are hypotheses used in steps 1.1 and 1.3, not limiting conclusions of the proof.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), inherited from the statement of [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]], whose distributional jump lemma uses it; declared in the Statement and carried by the citation of step 1.1.
Clause 4's equality case is an equivalence: step 1.4 proves $\Delta K\le0$ and the exact vanishing condition $e=1$ or $v_2^-=v_1^-$.
The converse of the vanishing case is the same equivalence, established in step 1.4 through the factor $(1-e^2)\mu\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2/2$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport theorem. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, let $\chi$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]) with spatial velocity $u$, let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3$ be an open set containing the swept region

$$\Sigma:=\bigl\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\bigr\}.$$

Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be of class $C^1$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); call it a **density field**. A **material subregion** is a nonempty bounded open $B'\subseteq B$ with $\overline{B'}\subseteq B$ ([[def-cm-material-region-and-density]]); for such $B'$ the same $\chi$ is a motion of $B'$.

**(i) Localization.** Assume for every material subregion $B'$ and every $t\in J_0$

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)\,dx=0, \tag{CM}$$

It is sufficient to assume this identity only for those pairs $(t,B')$ for which $\chi_t(B')$ is an open Euclidean ball with closure inside $\chi_t(B)$. Under either version of the conservation hypothesis,

$$\partial_t\rho(t,x)+\operatorname{div}\bigl(\rho u\bigr)(t,x)=0$$

for every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$, with the material derivative and divergence of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]].

**(ii) Converse.** Conversely, if $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ on an open neighbourhood of $\Sigma$ in $U$, then (CM) holds for every material subregion $B'$ and every $t\in J_0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, let $\chi$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$ and material derivative $D_t$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]], [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]]), let $J_0\subseteq I$ be an open interval with $\overline{J_0}\subseteq I$, and let $U$ contain the swept region $\Sigma=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\chi_t(\overline B)\}$.

Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ be a $C^1$ density field, let $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be a $C^1$ field (the stress field of [[def-cm-traction-and-stress]]), and let $b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Suppose:

**(K)** $\rho$ satisfies $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ at every $(t,x)$ with $t\in J_0$ and $x\in\chi_t(B)$;

**(L)** for every material subregion $B'$ (nonempty bounded open with $\overline{B'}\subseteq B$) and every $t\in J_0$ for which $\chi_t(B')$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) , the balance is

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)u(t,x)\,dx=\int_{\chi_t(B')}\rho(t,x)b(t,x)\,dx+\int_{\partial\chi_t(B')}\sigma(t,y)\,\nu(y)\,dS(y),$$

where $\nu$ is the outward unit normal and the surface integral is that of [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]].

Define the **row divergence** of $\sigma$ componentwise by

Then for every $(t,x)\in J_0\times\chi_t(B)$,

A **traction field** is a map $$t:S^2\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,$$ read with the following convention: $t(n)$ is the force per unit area exerted **by the material on the side towards which $n$ points upon the material on the other side**, at the point of a surface whose unit normal is $n$. The dependence of $t$ on position and time is suppressed in this notation; a traction **field on a set** $\Omega\times I$ is a map $t:\Omega\times I\times S^2\to\mathbb R^3$, and all statements below apply to each fixed $(y,s)$. A matrix $\sigma\in M_3(\mathbb R)$ ([[def-matrix-space]]) **represents** the traction field $t$ when $$t(n)=\sigma n\qquad\text{for every }n\in S^2,$$ the product being matrix-vector multiplication ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]). Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]), as used by the transport and divergence theorems. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open interval, let $B\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a material region, let $\chi$ be a motion of $B$ on $I$ with spatial velocity $u$, let $J_0\subseteq I$ have compact closure in $I$, and let $U$ contain the swept region of $B$ over $\overline{J_0}$ ([[def-cm-continuum-motion]]).

Let $\rho:U\to(0,\infty)$ and $\sigma:U\to M_3(\mathbb R)$ be $C^1$ and let $b:U\to\mathbb R^3$ be continuous. Define $g_i:=\sum_j\partial_j\sigma_{ij}$ and suppose, on $U$:

$$\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0\qquad\text{and}\qquad\rho\,D_tu=\rho b+g . \tag{KM}$$

Let $\psi:I\times O'\to\mathbb R^3$ be a second motion of a material region $B'\subseteq B$ (with the same reference chart domain $O'=O$ used for $B$; write $w$ for its spatial velocity), and suppose that for every $t\in J_0$ the control region $C_t:=\psi_t(B')$ is a bounded $C^1$ domain ([[def-bounded-c-one-domain-boundary-charts-and-outward-normal]]) with outward unit normal $\nu$ and boundary surface integral as in [[def-surface-integral-on-a-compact-c-one-hypersurface]].

Assume also that the control sweep $\Sigma_C:=\{(t,x):t\in\overline{J_0},\ x\in\psi_t(\overline{B'})\}$ is contained in $U$. Thus the fields and the local equations (KM) are defined on a neighbourhood of every closed control region. No condition that the control motion coincide with the material motion is imposed.

Then for every $t\in J_0$:

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C_t}\rho\,dx=-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,dS, \tag{CV1}$$

and componentwise

$$\frac{d}{dt}\int_{C_t}\rho u_i\,dx=\int_{C_t}\rho b_i\,dx+\Bigl(\int_{\partial C_t}\sigma\nu\,dS\Bigr)_i-\int_{\partial C_t}\rho u_i\,(u-w)\cdot\nu\,dS\qquad(i=1,2,3). \tag{CV2}$$

A **motion of $B$ on $I$** consists of an open set $O\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ with $\overline B\subseteq O$ ([[def-metric-ball]]) together with a map $$\chi:I\times O\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3$$ such that: 1. $\chi$ is of class $C^2$ ([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]); 2. for every $t\in I$ the map $\chi_t:=\chi(t,\cdot):O\to\mathbb R^3$ is of class $C^1$, is injective, and has $D_X\chi_t(X)$ invertible for every $X\in O$; 3. writing $$J(t,X):=\det\bigl(D_X\chi_t(X)\bigr)$$ with the determinant of [[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]], one has $J(t,X)>0$ for every $(t,X)\in I\times B$. We call $X\in B$ the **material label** (reference position), $x=\chi(t,X)$ the **position** at time $t$ of the label $X$, and $$\Omega_t:=\chi_t(B)$$ the **current (material) region** at time $t$. Condition 2 makes each $\chi_t:O\to\chi_t(O)$ a $C^1$ diffeomorphism onto the open set $\chi_t(O)$ ([[cor-injective-regular-ck-map-is-a-ck-diffeomorphism-onto-its-image]]). The **spatial velocity field** of the motion is $$u:\{(t,x):t\in I,\ x\in\chi_t(O)\}\longrightarrow\mathbb R^3,\qquad u\bigl(t,\chi(t,X)\bigr):=\partial_t\chi(t,X),$$ and the **spatial acceleration field** is the material derivative of $u$ in the sense of [[def-cm-euclidean-spatial-calculus]], $$a(t,x):=D_tu(t,x)=\partial_tu(t,x)+Du(t,x)u(t,x).$$

A bounded $C^1$ domain is a nonempty bounded open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ whose boundary is locally, after a rigid change of coordinates, the graph $z=h(y)$ of a $C^1$ function, with $\Omega$ locally exactly the subgraph $z<h(y)$. Connectedness is not required. The outward normal in these coordinates is $\nu=(-Dh,1)/\sqrt{1+|Dh|^2}$, transported by the orthogonal coordinate map. Its overlap agreement is justified with surface charts below.

Let S be a compact embedded $C^1$ hypersurface in $\mathbb R^n$, $n\ge2$. Choose finitely many regular injective $C^1$ parametrizations $X_j:V_j\to S\cap O_j$ with $C^1$ coordinate transitions, and an ambient partition $\chi_j$ from [[lem-finite-ambient-partitions-for-euclidean-boundary-integration]], with supports compactly contained in the corresponding chart neighborhoods. Put $J_{X_j}=\sqrt{\det(DX_j^TDX_j)}$, using [[def-gram-matrix-and-gram-determinant]]. For a nonnegative Borel f on S define $\int_S f\,dS=\sum_j\int_{V_j}(\chi_j f)(X_j(y))J_{X_j}(y)\,dy$, where the integrals on the right are those of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]] and $0\cdot\infty=0$. Set $S(A)=\int_S\mathbf1_A\,dS$ for Borel A. For signed f with $\int_S|f|\,dS<\infty$ use the difference of the positive and negative integrals. The same chart formula restricts to a compact Borel face contained in a regular patch. The empty surface has zero integral.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$. Both integrals are finite, with the continuous interior derivative convention and the outward normal on every boundary component.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and let $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be maps. Suppose the two **material balance identities** $$m'(t)=r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t),\qquad (mv)'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)$$ hold for every $t\in I$, where $mv$ denotes the pointwise scalar multiple. Then $$m(t)v'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in I).$$ In particular, if $F\equiv0$, $r_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv0$ and $r_{\mathrm{out}}\equiv r$ for a constant $r\ge0$, then $mv'=-r(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$: the acceleration is governed by the momentum carried away per unit time relative to the body, not by $(mv)'=0$. The two balance identities are the **adopted content of the material momentum accounting** — the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,dt$ of matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,dt$ with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$". They are not derived here from any closed-system law; the deduction below is their product-rule consequence.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define $$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$ Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$ the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$. The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The **Euclidean norm** of $x$ is $$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$ which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and [[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by [[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable, and let $E\in\mathcal A$. Since [[prop-closure-properties-of-measurable-functions-used-by-the-integral]] implies that $f\chi_E$ is measurable, define the **integral of $f$ over $E$** by $$\int_E f\,d\mu:=\int f\chi_E\,d\mu,$$ where the integral on the right is the nonnegative Lebesgue integral of [[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]].

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$: | | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms | |---|---|---|---| | $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ | | $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ | | $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ | | $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ | | | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is **closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$, $[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$.

Let $k\in\mathbb N$, let $m,q\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be open, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$. A map $f:U\to\mathbb R^q$ is of class $C^k$ when each component is of class $C^k$. Each scalar component uses the word-derivative convention of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]], whose source dimension is positive. The map is **smooth**, or $C^\infty$, when it is $C^k$ for every $k\in\mathbb N$.

**(i) Particle labels and worldlines.** A model of the framework has **particle labels** $i=1,\dots,N$ for some $N\ge1$. To each label and each *inertial frame* of the model — an adapted chart $(o,u,(e_{1},e_{2},e_{3}))$ with coordinates $(t,x)$ in the sense of [[post-cm01-frames]] — there is assigned a **worldline** $\gamma_{i}:I\to A$ described in that frame, where $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ is a nondegenerate open interval — that is, an interval of the form $(a,b)$ with $-\infty\le a<b\le+\infty$ and at least two points — the curve $\gamma_{i}$ is of class $C^{2}$ in the adapted coordinates of the frame, and the **parameter condition** $$\tau\bigl(\gamma_{i}(t)-o\bigr)=t\qquad(t\in I)$$ holds: the curve parameter is the elapsed time from the origin of the frame, so in the frame's coordinates $\gamma_{i}(t)=(t,x_{i}(t))$ with $x_{i}:I\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{2}$. The parameter condition replaces the causal conditions of relativistic kinematics: no timelike condition on the velocity and no upper bound on its Euclidean norm is imposed, and the parameter is not free up to reparametrization.

**(d) Dimensions of the quantities of this framework.** The dimension map is fixed on the following quantities: 1. coordinates: $[t]=\tau$ and $[x_{i}]=\ell$; 2. velocity components: $[w_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$; 3. acceleration components: $[a_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-2}$; 4. mass: $[m]=\mu$, and the mass operator (multiplication of spatial components by masses) has dimension $\mu$; 5. angles and entries of rotation matrices: dimensionless, $[R_{ij}]=1$ for $R\in SO(3)$ under the radian convention, in which an angle is the ratio of an arc length to a radius and therefore a ratio of two lengths; 6. the standard derived quantities have the dimensions obtained from the rules of (b) once their defining relations are stated: momentum $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$, force $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$, energy $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$, action $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$, angular momentum $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$;

derivations.claim: Local forms: the adopted smooth admissible subregions include the inverse images under $\chi_t$ of all sufficiently small current balls with closure in the field domain. Thus the current-ball localization variant of [L1] applies to the adopted material mass balance and gives $\partial_t\rho+\operatorname{div}(\rho u)=0$ on the swept region over $J_0$, and with the adopted momentum balance on these smooth admissible test regions, the local momentum theorem of [L1] gives $\rho D_tu=\rho b+g$ there, with $g$ the row divergence of the $C^1$ field $\sigma$.

Clause 1: by the control-sweep hypothesis, the fields are defined on an open neighbourhood of each closed control region. If the sweep lies locally inside the current material region, step 1.1 supplies (K) and (KM) on that neighbourhood; otherwise the same local equations there are explicit adopted hypotheses. Thus in either case all field-domain and local-equation conditions of [L2] hold for the control motion $\psi$, and [L2] gives (CV1) and (CV2) for every $t\in J_0$.

Clause 2: if $\psi=\chi$ then $w=u$ on $\partial C_t$, so $(u-w)\cdot\nu=0$ and both flux integrals in (CV1) and (CV2) vanish; the identities become the material balances of the model. If $\psi$ is constant then $w=0$ and $u-w=u$, giving the displayed fixed-region equations with $m_C$, $P_C$; when in addition the fields are steady and $C$ is fixed, the left sides are the rates of the steady-flow treatment and the equations reduce to the balance between the external force and the momentum flux difference.

Clause 3, mass balance: decomposing $\partial C_t$ into the inlet, outlet and zero-flux pieces, the boundary term of (CV1) becomes $-\int_{\partial C_t}ho(u-w)\cdot
u =-\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{in}}}ho(u-w)\cdot
u-\int_{\Sigma_{\mathrm{out}}}ho(u-w)\cdot

citations.quote: **(ii) The collinear restitution contact law.** A model run in the isolated reciprocal impulse model at $t_*$ is **collinear** when there is a unit vector $n\in\mathbb R^3$ (the **contact direction**) with $v_i^{\pm}\parallel n$ for $i=1,2$ and $\langle v_2^--v_1^-,n\rangle<0$ (the labels approach along $n$). For a collinear contact, adopt a **coefficient of restitution** $e\in[0,1]$ — a dimensionless model datum of the pair and the contact — and the **restitution law** $$v_2^+-v_1^+=-e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$ For $e=1$ the contact is called **elastic**, for $e=0$ **perfectly inelastic** and otherwise **semi-elastic**; the law is a constitutive assumption, not a consequence of the impulse equations of clause (i), and $e$ is not derived from the masses or the approach speed. The law is stated only for a single collinear contact; simultaneous contacts, repeated contacts and tangential (friction) impulses are outside the model.
For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$. This is the right-handed **cross product**.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The **Euclidean norm** of $x$ is $$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$ which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and [[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by [[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

Their principal inverses are denoted $$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$ and are characterised by $$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$ The chosen target intervals are part of the notation: without them, inverse sine and inverse cosine would be multivalued relations rather than functions. Their continuity follows from [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable ([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$ at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then: 1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$; 2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$; 3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$; 4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Let $(a_1,a_2)\subseteq(0,\infty)$ be an interval with at least two points, let $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ be of class $C^1$ with $\theta'(b)\ne0$ for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$ — a deflection branch with inverse $b:(\theta_1,\theta_2)\to(a_1,a_2)$ in the sense of [[def-cm-scattering-data]] — and let $g:(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and $2\pi$-periodic in its second argument. Then $$\int_{a_1}^{a_2}\!\int_0^{2\pi} g\bigl(\theta(b),\varphi\bigr)\,b\;\mathrm db\;\mathrm d\varphi =\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(\theta,\varphi)\,b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|\;\mathrm d\theta\;\mathrm d\varphi .$$ Consequently the outgoing angular measure carried to the branch has density $b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|$ with respect to $\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi$, and cross-section density $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta) =\frac{b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'(b(\theta))\bigr|}\qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2)$$ with respect to the solid-angle element $\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi$; the two expressions agree because $b'(\theta)=1/\theta'(b(\theta))$. For finitely many branches with pairwise disjoint images the contributions add.

**(i) The differential cross-section of a branch.** Let a central scattering model be given, let $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ be a **deflection branch** in the sense of [[def-cm-scattering-data]] — an interval $(a_1,a_2)$ of impact parameters with $\theta$ of class $C^1$ and $\theta'(b)\ne0$ — and suppose the branch **records the deflection** of the model: for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$ the scattering motion of the model with impact parameter $b$, energy $E$ and angular momentum $J$ has scattering angle $\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\theta(b)$. Write $(a_1,a_2)\ni b\mapsto\theta\in(\theta_1,\theta_2)$ for this bijection and $b(\theta):=\theta^{-1}(\theta)$ for its inverse ([[def-cm-scattering-data]]). The **differential cross-section of the branch** is the function $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta):=\frac{b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'\bigl(b(\theta)\bigr)\bigr|}\qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2),$$ the cross-section density of [[def-cm-scattering-data]].

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $G : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at every point of $[a,b]$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]; at $a$ and $b$ this is the one-sided derivative), let $f := G'$, and suppose $f$ is integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]). Then $$\int_a^b f \;=\; G(b) - G(a) .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$: | | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms | |---|---|---|---| | $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ | | $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ | | $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ | | $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ | | | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is **closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$, $[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$.

derivations.claim: Reflection and conservation: by [L1], $|v^+|=|v^-|=v_\infty$ and the angular momentum about the centre is conserved across the contact; hence the two free pieces of the motion are straight lines and the motion has a constant angular momentum $j$ with $|j|=\mu b v_\infty$, so the impact parameter of the incoming line is indeed $b=J/(\mu v_\infty)$ in the sense of [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] clause (ii).

Deflection: let $\alpha$ be the acute angle between the inward normal $-n$ at first contact and the incoming direction $\hat u$, so that $\sin\alpha=b/a$ by [L2]. The reflection turns the velocity by the angle computed in [L2], namely $\pi-2\alpha$; since $b\in(0,a)$ we have $\alpha\in(0,\pi/2)$ and $\theta=\pi-2\alpha\in(0,\pi)$.

Branch and inverse: the map $b\mapsto\theta(b)=\pi-2\arcsin(b/a)$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,a)$ by [L3] and its image is $(0,\pi)$; solving $\sin((\pi-\theta)/2)=b/a$ gives $b(\theta)=a\cos(\theta/2)$ on $(0,\pi)$, which is $C^1$ with $b'(\theta)=-\frac{a}{2}\sin(\theta/2)\ne0$. Thus the model realises a single deflection branch with image $(0,\pi)$, and no branch sum is needed for it.

Cross-section density: by [L4], $\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta)=\frac{b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{a\cos(\theta/2)\cdot\frac{a}{2}\sin(\theta/2)}{\sin\theta}$. Using $\sin\theta=2\sin(\theta/2)\cos(\theta/2)$ this equals $\frac{a^2}{4}$ for every $\theta\in(0,\pi)$: the outgoing angular distribution is uniform, and the density is finite, positive and independent of $\theta$.

Truncated total: by [L4] and the fundamental theorem, for the full image interval $$\sigma\bigl((0,\pi)\bigr)=\int_0^{\pi}\frac{a^2}{4}\,2\pi\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta=\frac{a^2}{4}\cdot2\pi\cdot\bigl[-\cos\theta\bigr]_0^{\pi} =\frac{a^2}{4}\cdot 4\pi=\pi a^2,$$ and for $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ the band value is $\frac{a^2}{4}\cdot2\pi(\cos\theta_1-\cos\theta_2)$, finite; in particular the branch has a finite ideal total $\pi a^2$.

Model boundary: the motion just computed is piecewise linear with a contact rule, not a central-force trajectory of class $C^2$ with a finite-range potential; the quadrature theorem [[pthm-cm15-central-scattering]] does not apply to it, and the finite total $\pi a^2$ is a property of this contact model, not a counterexample to the forward divergence of the ideal Coulomb branch. The declared data are model data: no measurement is reported, and the agreement of the algebraic form with the cited impenetrable-sphere computation is a consistency check of the model, not evidence about nature.

citations.quote: 2. **(Global non-colliding scattering motion.)** Let $r:J_0\to\mathbb R^3$ be the relative coordinate of a motion of the model with attached angular momentum $j=\mu\,r\times r'=Je_3$ and energy $E$, with $|r(t)|\ge r_*$ for every $t\in J_0$ and $|r(t_*)|=r_*$ for some $t_*\in J_0$. Then $r$ extends uniquely to a central-force trajectory $\bar r:\mathbb R\to \mathbb R^3$ whose extension is the relative coordinate of a motion of the two-label model on all of $\mathbb R$; $\rho:=|\bar r|$ satisfies $\rho\ge r_*>0$ (no collision), $\rho(t)>r_*$ for $t\ne t_*$, and $\rho$ is strictly decreasing on $(-\infty,t_*]$ and strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$; the asymptotic velocities $v_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty} \bar r'(t)$ exist with $|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}=:v_\infty$, and the asymptotic perpendicular distance of each branch to its limiting direction equals $b=J/(\mu v_\infty)=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}$, so that $J=\mu b\,v_\infty$. Unlike the finite-range case, there is no radius beyond which the motion is exactly free: the limits above are asymptotic. 3. **(Deflection and its single branch.)** With polar data $(\rho,\theta)$ in a triad with $e_3=j/J$, the half-angle of the motion is $$\Delta=\frac{\pi}{2}-\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}\in\Bigl(0,\frac{\pi}{2}\Bigr),$$ its scattering angle is $$\theta_{\mathrm s}=\pi-2\Delta=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}\in(0,\pi),$$ and its signed velocity rotation is $2\Delta-\pi=-2\arctan(\kappa/(2Eb))$. The **deflection map** $$\theta_{\mathrm{def}}:(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi),\qquad \theta_{\mathrm{def}}(b):=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb},$$ is $C^1$ and strictly decreasing, hence a $C^1$ bijection with inverse $b(\theta)=\dfrac{\kappa}{2E}\cot\dfrac{\theta}{2}$; it is a single deflection branch of the model on $(0,\infty)$ with $\theta_{\mathrm{def}}'(b)\ne0$ everywhere and no wrapping ($0<\Delta<\pi/2$ for every $b>0$). 4. **(Cross-section, angular cutoffs and divergence.)** The differential cross-section of that branch is $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta)=\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2\csc^4\frac{\theta}{2}\qquad(0<\theta<\pi),$$ finite and positive; for $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ the truncated total cross-section over the angular band is the finite number $$\sigma\bigl((\theta_1,\theta_2)\bigr) =\pi\bigl(b(\theta_1)^2-b(\theta_2)^2\bigr),$$ and by monotonicity the band $\theta\ge\theta_1$ has $\sigma\bigl((\theta_1,\pi)\bigr)=\pi b(\theta_1)^2 =\pi\bigl(\frac{\kappa}{2E}\bigr)^2\cot^2\frac{\theta_1}{2}$; whereas the truncated integral over $(0,\theta_0)$ diverges for every $\theta_0\in(0,\pi)$, so the **ideal total cross-section of the model does not exist**. Every positive angular cutoff therefore yields a finite truncated cross-section, and the model is predictive only jointly with an angular acceptance.

Let $\mu>0$, $\kappa>0$, $E>0$ and $J>0$, write $b:=J/\sqrt{2\mu E}>0$ for the asymptotic impact distance of [[thm-cm-coulomb-scattering]], and define the **deflection map** $$\theta_{\rm def}:(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi),\qquad \theta_{\rm def}(b):=2\arctan\frac{\kappa}{2Eb}.$$ Then: 1. $\theta_{\rm def}$ is $C^1$ and strictly decreasing, with $\theta_{\rm def}(b)\to\pi$ as $b\downarrow0$ and $\theta_{\rm def}(b)\to0$ as $b\to\infty$; it is a $C^1$ bijection $(0,\infty)\to(0,\pi)$ with inverse $$b(\theta)=\frac{\kappa}{2E}\cot\frac{\theta}{2}\qquad(0<\theta<\pi).$$ 2. For every interval $(\theta_1,\theta_2)\subseteq(0,\pi)$ the pair $(\theta,b)$ is a deflection branch with cross-section density $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta) =b(\theta)\Bigl|\frac{\mathrm db}{\mathrm d\theta}(\theta)\Bigr|\frac{1}{\sin\theta} =\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2\csc^4\frac{\theta}{2},$$ finite and positive on $(\theta_1,\theta_2)$; and the pushforward of the incident flux measure under the branch is described by [[thm-cm-differential-cross-section-density]]. 3. For every $\theta_0\in(0,\pi)$ the truncated total cross-section $$\int_0^{\theta_0}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\Bigl(\frac{\kappa}{4E}\Bigr)^2 \csc^4\frac{\theta}{2}\,\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi\,\mathrm d\theta=+\infty,$$ while for $0<\theta_1<\theta_2<\pi$ the integral over $(\theta_1,\theta_2)\times(0,2\pi)$ is finite; in this sense the total cross-section of the ideal Coulomb model diverges at forward angles and every finite angular acceptance cuts it off.

Then the momentum curves $p_i=m_ix_i'$ are of class $C^1$ on $I$; in particular $$p_i(t_*^+)=p_i(t_*^-)\qquad(i=1,2),$$ so $J=0$: no motion of that class carries a nonzero isolated impulse. The finite-jump model of [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (i) is therefore a genuine extension of the smooth-force branch, not one of its cases. 3. **(Collinear restitution solution.)** Suppose in addition that the contact is collinear with contact direction $n$ and coefficient of restitution $e\in[0,1]$ ([[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (ii)). Then $$J=\mu(1+e)\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr),$$ $J$ is parallel to $n$, the centre-of-mass velocity $V:=M^{-1}(m_1v_1^-+m_2v_2^-)$ is unchanged across the impact, and the post-impact velocities are $$v_1^+=V+\frac{m_2}{M}\,e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr),\qquad v_2^+=V-\frac{m_1}{M}\,e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$ 4. **(Kinetic energy of the impact.)** The kinetic-energy change across the impact is $$\Delta K:=\frac{m_1\lVert v_1^+\rVert_2^2+m_2\lVert v_2^+\rVert_2^2}{2} -\frac{m_1\lVert v_1^-\rVert_2^2+m_2\lVert v_2^-\rVert_2^2}{2} =-\frac{1-e^2}{2}\,\mu\,\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2\le0,$$ with equality if and only if $e=1$ or $v_2^-=v_1^-$. For $0\le e<1$ the contact model is dissipative: the total kinetic energy of the two labels is not conserved across the impact, and the deficit $\frac{1-e^2}{2}\mu\lVert v_2^--v_1^-\rVert_2^2$ is a quantity of the adopted contact law.

citations.quote: **(iii) The open-body material accounting.** Adopt for a body whose mass, velocity, external force and exchanged matter are described by maps $m:I\to(0,\infty)$, $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ (mass rates and *inertial* velocities of the matter entering and leaving, measured in the same inertial frame as $v$) the **material balance identities** $$m'=r_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}},\qquad (mv)'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}\,w_{\mathrm{in}}-r_{\mathrm{out}}\,w_{\mathrm{out}} .$$ They are the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,\mathrm dt$ of matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,\mathrm dt$ with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$", and they are adopted rather than derived from a closed-system law. Their product-rule consequence $mv'=F+r_{\mathrm{in}}(w_{\mathrm{in}}-v)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$ is proved in [[thm-cm-variable-mass-momentum-balance]]; in particular the closed-system law $(mv)'=F$ is recovered only when $r_{\mathrm{in}}w_{\mathrm{in}}=r_{\mathrm{out}}w_{\mathrm{out}}$. The model parameters $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}},w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}$ are model data with $[r_{\mathrm{in}}]=[r_{\mathrm{out}}]=\mathsf M\tau^{-1}$ and $[w_{\mathrm{in}}]=[w_{\mathrm{out}}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]), let $m:I\to(0,\infty)$ and $v:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable ([[def-derivative]], [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]), and let $F:I\to\mathbb R^3$, $r_{\mathrm{in}},r_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to[0,\infty)$ and $w_{\mathrm{in}},w_{\mathrm{out}}:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be maps. Suppose the two **material balance identities** $$m'(t)=r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t),\qquad (mv)'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)$$ hold for every $t\in I$, where $mv$ denotes the pointwise scalar multiple. Then $$m(t)v'(t)=F(t)+r_{\mathrm{in}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{in}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)-r_{\mathrm{out}}(t)\bigl(w_{\mathrm{out}}(t)-v(t)\bigr)\qquad(t\in I).$$ In particular, if $F\equiv0$, $r_{\mathrm{in}}\equiv0$ and $r_{\mathrm{out}}\equiv r$ for a constant $r\ge0$, then $mv'=-r(w_{\mathrm{out}}-v)$: the acceleration is governed by the momentum carried away per unit time relative to the body, not by $(mv)'=0$. The two balance identities are the **adopted content of the material momentum accounting** — the mathematical rendering of "gains $r_{\mathrm{in}}\,dt$ of matter with velocity $w_{\mathrm{in}}$, loses $r_{\mathrm{out}}\,dt$ with velocity $w_{\mathrm{out}}$, and feels the external force $F$". They are not derived here from any closed-system law; the deduction below is their product-rule consequence.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a **limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function $$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$ The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives $x - c \ne 0$. **The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.** For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so $$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$ and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So $q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines. $f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the **derivative of $f$ at $c$** is $$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$
