citations.quote: **(i) The isolated reciprocal impulse model.** A two-label force model with masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), time window $I_0$, configuration domain $Q$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]) and continuous external-plus-pair force maps $F_1,F_2$ is **run in the isolated reciprocal impulse model at $t_*\in I_0$** when there is a motion $x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ of the associated first-order system ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]) such that: 1. $x_1,x_2$ are continuous on $I$ and twice continuously differentiable on each of $I\cap(-\infty,t_*)$ and $I\cap(t_*,\infty)$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and $m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ for every $t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}$; 2. the one-sided limits $v_i^{\pm}:=\lim_{t\to t_*\pm}x_i'(t)$ exist in $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); 3. there is a vector $J\in\mathbb R^3$, the **impulse**, with $$m_1\bigl(v_1^+-v_1^-\bigr)=J,\qquad m_2\bigl(v_2^+-v_2^-\bigr)=-J .$$ The two equations of clause 3 are the **reciprocal finite-jump form** of the isolated impulse: the two labels receive equal and opposite momentum changes. The model places no bound on the force maps across $t_*$; its distributional rendering by test-function pairings is proved in [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]]. The dimension of the impulse is $[J]=\mathsf M\ell\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). **(ii) The collinear restitution contact law.** A model run in the isolated reciprocal impulse model at $t_*$ is **collinear** when there is a unit vector $n\in\mathbb R^3$ (the **contact direction**) with $v_i^{\pm}\parallel n$ for $i=1,2$ and $\langle v_2^--v_1^-,n\rangle<0$ (the labels approach along $n$). For a collinear contact, adopt a **coefficient of restitution** $e\in[0,1]$ — a dimensionless model datum of the pair and the contact — and the **restitution law** $$v_2^+-v_1^+=-e\,\bigl(v_2^--v_1^-\bigr).$$ For $e=1$ the contact is called **elastic**, for $e=0$ **perfectly inelastic** and otherwise **semi-elastic**; the law is a constitutive assumption, not a consequence of the impulse equations of clause (i), and $e$ is not derived from the masses or the approach speed. The law is stated only for a single collinear contact; simultaneous contacts, repeated contacts and tangential (friction) impulses are outside the model.

**(ii) Scattering motions and their data.** Let $r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$ with values $|r(t)|\in J_0$ and with constant angular momentum $j=\mu\,r\times r'=Je_3\ne0$ for $J>0$ and an oriented orthonormal triad $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ ([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]], [[thm-cm-central-force-angular-momentum-conservation]], [[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]], [[lem-cm-oriented-orthonormal-triads]]). Call $r$ a **scattering motion** of the model when it satisfies the hypotheses under which the page's scattering theorems establish the limits below. Its **energy** is the constant $$E:=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+u(\lvert r\rvert)>0$$ of [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]] (constant by [[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]] clause 4), its **asymptotic velocities** are the limits $$v_-:=\lim_{t\to-\infty}r'(t),\qquad v_+:=\lim_{t\to+\infty}r'(t),$$ taken in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]] (their existence under the hypotheses is a theorem, not a convention), and its **scattering speed** is $$v_\infty:=\lVert v_-\rVert_2=\lVert v_+\rVert_2=\sqrt{2E/\mu},$$ the equality being part of the scattering theorems. The **incoming branch** is the trajectory restricted to times before its apsis; the **impact parameter** is the perpendicular distance from the force centre of the line through the incoming branch, defined by $$b:=\frac{\lVert r(t)\times v_-\rVert_2}{\lVert v_-\rVert_2} \qquad(t\ \text{on the incoming branch}),$$ with $\times$ the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; the value is independent of $t$ because $r\times r'=j/\mu$ is constant, and the scattering theorems identify it with the geometric distance, giving $b=J/(\mu v_\infty)$. Its dimension is $[b]=\ell$. **(iii) Polar advance and deflection conventions.** Fix polar data $(\rho,\theta)$ of the scattering motion in the triad, $r=\rho\,n(\theta)$, $n(\varphi):=\cos\varphi\,e_1+\sin\varphi\,e_2$ ([[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]), and let $t_*$ be an apsis time, $|r(t_*)|=\min_t|r(t)|$. The **polar advance of one half** is $$\Delta:=\theta(+\infty)-\theta(t_*)=\theta(t_*)-\theta(-\infty),$$ defined by the limits asserted in the scattering theorems, and the **polar advance of the motion** is $2\Delta$. The **scattering angle** is the undirected angle between the asymptotic velocity directions, $$\theta_{\mathrm{s}}:=\arccos\!\left(\frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{\lVert v_-\rVert_2\,\lVert v_+\rVert_2}\right)\in[0,\pi],$$ equivalently the angle between the incoming and outgoing asymptote lines; the **signed velocity rotation** is the continuous rotation angle of $r'(t)$, measured counterclockwise about $e_3$ relative to the incoming direction, so that a positive value is a counterclockwise turn. The scattering theorems give $\cos\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\cos(\pi-2\Delta)$ and the signed rotation $2\Delta-\pi$; in particular, when $0<\Delta<\pi/2$ the scattering angle is $$\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi),$$ while for $\Delta\ge\pi/2$ the motion has wrapped past the backward direction and $\theta_{\mathrm{s}}$ is the wrapped value $\arccos(\cos(\pi-2\Delta))$.
For $u=(u_x,u_y,u_z)$ and $v=(v_x,v_y,v_z)$ in $\mathbb R^3$, define $u\times v=(u_yv_z-u_zv_y,\,u_zv_x-u_xv_z,\,u_xv_y-u_yv_x)$. This is the right-handed **cross product**.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The **Euclidean norm** of $x$ is $$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$ which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and [[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by [[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The **Euclidean norm** of $x$ is $$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$ which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and [[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by [[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

Their principal inverses are denoted $$\arcsin:[-1,1]\to[-\pi/2,\pi/2],\qquad\arccos:[-1,1]\to[0,\pi],$$ and are characterised by $$\sin(\arcsin y)=y,\qquad\cos(\arccos y)=y\qquad(-1\le y\le1).$$ The chosen target intervals are part of the notation: without them, inverse sine and inverse cosine would be multivalued relations rather than functions. Their continuity follows from [[thm-continuous-inverse]].

Sine is strictly increasing on each interval $[-\pi/2+2m\pi,\pi/2+2m\pi]$ and strictly decreasing on each interval $[\pi/2+2m\pi,3\pi/2+2m\pi]$. Cosine is strictly decreasing on $[2m\pi,(2m+1)\pi]$ and strictly increasing on $[(2m+1)\pi,(2m+2)\pi]$. Both functions have range $[-1,1]$.

For every real $x$, $\sin ^2x+\cos ^2x=1$, $\sin(-x)=-\sin x$, and $\cos(-x)=\cos x$. Wherever the displayed quotients are defined, $\tan(-x)=-\tan x$, $\cot(-x)=-\cot x$, $\sec(-x)=\sec x$, $\csc(-x)=-\csc x$, $1+\tan^2x=\sec^2x$, and $1+\cot^2x=\csc^2x$.

Let $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]), let $f : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $I$ ([[def-continuity-real]]) and differentiable at every point of $I$ interior to $I$ ([[def-interior-closure-boundary-r]], [[def-derivative]]). The words *nondecreasing*, *increasing*, *nonincreasing* and *decreasing* are those of [[def-monotone-function]], in which *increasing* is the strict notion. 1. If $f'(x) \ge 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is nondecreasing on $I$. 2. If $f'(x) > 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is increasing on $I$. 3. If $f'(x) \le 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is nonincreasing on $I$. 4. If $f'(x) < 0$ at every interior point $x$ of $I$, then $f$ is decreasing on $I$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]], [[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy $$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$ Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with $g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite $f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable ([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$ at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$ ([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then: 1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$; 2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$; 3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$; 4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$: | | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms | |---|---|---|---| | $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ | | $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ | | $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ | | $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ | | | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ | An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is **closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$, $[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with $$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

This item fixes the **scattering data** of the restricted model class of
[[post-cm05-central-model]] and the preparation conventions in which the
scattering statements of this page are phrased. All objects are model data;
nothing here is a measured value.

**(i) The scattering model.** A **central scattering model** is a model of
class (i) of [[post-cm05-central-model]] with $N=2$ labels, masses
$m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), no external forces, and a
static central pair potential $u\in C^2(J_0)$
([[def-cm-scattering-data]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]])
whose collision-excluded interval satisfies $(0,\infty)\subseteq J_0$, so
that the only forbidden configuration is the collision $r=0$. Its **reduced
problem** is the one-label problem of class (ii) with reduced mass
$\mu:=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$ ([[def-cm01-units]]: $[\mu]=\mathsf M$) and the same
potential, presented through the relative coordinate $r=x_1-x_2$; by
[[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]] the relative coordinate of every motion of
the model is a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ and every pair of an
affine centre-of-mass motion and a solution of the reduced equation on a
common interval reconstructs a motion of the model.

**(ii) Scattering motions and their data.** Let $r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$
be a central-force trajectory for $(\mu,u)$ defined on all of $\mathbb R$
with values $|r(t)|\in J_0$ and with constant angular momentum
$j=\mu\,r\times r'=Je_3\ne0$ for $J>0$ and an oriented orthonormal triad
$(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ ([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]],
[[thm-cm-central-force-angular-momentum-conservation]],
[[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]],
[[lem-cm-oriented-orthonormal-triads]]). Call $r$ a **scattering motion** of
the model when it satisfies the hypotheses under which the page's scattering
theorems establish the limits below. Its **energy** is the constant
$$E:=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+u(\lvert r\rvert)>0$$
of [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]] (constant by
[[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]] clause 4), its **asymptotic
velocities** are the limits
$$v_-:=\lim_{t\to-\infty}r'(t),\qquad v_+:=\lim_{t\to+\infty}r'(t),$$
taken in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]
(their existence under the hypotheses is a theorem, not a convention), and
its **scattering speed** is
$$v_\infty:=\lVert v_-\rVert_2=\lVert v_+\rVert_2=\sqrt{2E/\mu},$$
the equality being part of the scattering theorems. The **incoming branch**
is the trajectory restricted to times before its apsis; the **impact
parameter** is the perpendicular distance from the force centre of the line
through the incoming branch, defined by
$$b:=\frac{\lVert r(t)\times v_-\rVert_2}{\lVert v_-\rVert_2} \qquad(t\ \text{on the incoming branch}),$$
with $\times$ the cross product of [[def-cross-product-in-r3]] and the
Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]; the value is independent
of $t$ because $r\times r'=j/\mu$ is constant, and the scattering theorems
identify it with the geometric distance, giving $b=J/(\mu v_\infty)$. Its
dimension is $[b]=\ell$.

**(iii) Polar advance and deflection conventions.** Fix polar data
$(\rho,\theta)$ of the scattering motion in the triad, $r=\rho\,n(\theta)$,
$n(\varphi):=\cos\varphi\,e_1+\sin\varphi\,e_2$
([[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]), and let $t_*$ be an apsis time,
$|r(t_*)|=\min_t|r(t)|$. The **polar advance of one half** is
$$\Delta:=\theta(+\infty)-\theta(t_*)=\theta(t_*)-\theta(-\infty),$$
defined by the limits asserted in the scattering theorems, and the
**polar advance of the motion** is $2\Delta$. The **scattering angle** is the
undirected angle between the asymptotic velocity directions,
$$\theta_{\mathrm{s}}:=\arccos\!\left(\frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{\lVert v_-\rVert_2\,\lVert v_+\rVert_2}\right)\in[0,\pi],$$
equivalently the angle between the incoming and outgoing asymptote lines;
the **signed velocity rotation** is the continuous rotation angle of
$r'(t)$, measured counterclockwise about $e_3$ relative to the incoming
direction, so that a positive value is a counterclockwise turn. The scattering
theorems give $\cos\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\cos(\pi-2\Delta)$ and the signed
rotation $2\Delta-\pi$; in particular, when $0<\Delta<\pi/2$ the scattering
angle is
$$\theta_{\mathrm{s}}=\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi),$$
while for $\Delta\ge\pi/2$ the motion has wrapped past the backward direction
and $\theta_{\mathrm{s}}$ is the wrapped value $\arccos(\cos(\pi-2\Delta))$.
The **deflection map** of a scattering model is the partial map
$b\mapsto\theta_{\mathrm{s}}(b)$ carrying the impact parameter of each
scattering motion that satisfies the hypotheses to its scattering angle;
the scattering theorems of the page determine its values on the hypotheses
they state, and **deflection branches** of it are the $C^1$ branches of
[[def-cm-scattering-data]].

**(iv) The uniform-incident preparation (adopted model datum).** The
**uniform-incident preparation** of a central scattering model with cutoff
$b_{\max}>0$ and flux $\Phi>0$ is the following adopted model of a scattering
experiment for the reduced problem: independent incident reduced labels, each
with energy $E>0$, angular momentum $Je_3$ and impact-azimuth pair
distributed with density $b\,\mathrm db\,\mathrm d\varphi$ on
$(0,b_{\max})\times(0,2\pi)$ normalised to unit total mass, where the
**incident flux** $\Phi$ is the number of incident labels per unit area per
unit time and $[\Phi]=\ell^{-2}\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). Under this
preparation the model predicts the expected rate
$$\dot N(A)= \Phi\cdot\nu(A)$$
of incident labels whose impact-azimuth pair lies in $A$, where $\nu$ is the
incident flux measure of [[def-cm-scattering-data]]; the rate of scattered
labels into a solid-angle set is the flux times the pushforward of $\nu$ under
the deflection map, whose density on a branch is the cross-section density
introduced in this page's cross-section definition. This is a predicted model
quantity: it reports no
detection, and its comparison with data requires a separately specified
experiment, apparatus model and statistical analysis.

**(v) Reading conventions.** All angles and lengths above are data of the
**relative** problem, equivalently of the centre-of-mass frame of the
two-label model: the relative coordinate $r$ and the centre of mass $X$ are
those of clause (i) and [[def-cm03-centre-of-mass-and-momenta]]. The
individual labels move along $x_1=X+\frac{m_2}{M}r$ and
$x_2=X-\frac{m_1}{M}r$ with $M=m_1+m_2$
([[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]] clause 4), so their directions relative to
the centre of mass differ from $r$ by the mass factors and generally differ
from each other; an angle of the reduced problem is not, without further
computation, an angle of either label with respect to a laboratory frame.
"Target", "projectile" and "detector" are names for model components and
carry no empirical claim.

**(vi) Exclusions and status.** The class excludes velocity- or
time-dependent, non-central and non-potential forces; constraints and
reaction forces; collisions $r=0$; external forces; and models with more than
two labels, exactly as in [[post-cm05-central-model]] clause (v). The
preparation of clause (iv) is one adopted idealisation among many; the
scattering theorems state separately which potentials, energies and angular
momenta produce the data of clauses (ii)-(iii). The quantities $\mu$, $u$
(with any parameters it carries), $E$, $J$, $b$, $b_{\max}$, $\Phi$ are model
data; quantitative empirical use requires separately stated measured inputs
with uncertainties, and no statement of this page asserts that any physical
system is exactly a central scattering model or that any beam is exactly
uniform.

**Why the objects are defined.** The relative coordinate is a central-force
trajectory by the cited reduction theorem; the attached energy and angular
momentum are defined by [[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]] and are constant
on the trajectory by [[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]] clause 4 and
[[thm-cm-central-force-angular-momentum-conservation]]; the impact parameter
is $t$-independent because $r\times r'=j/\mu$ is constant; and the
preparation measure of clause (iv) is the measure $\nu$ of
[[def-cm-scattering-data]]. The arccosine of clause (iii) is defined because
the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives
$|\langle v_-,v_+\rangle|/(\lVert v_-\rVert_2\lVert v_+\rVert_2)\le1$
([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**Mathematical status.** The vocabulary is attached to the adopted model
class of [[post-cm05-central-model]]; the existence of the limits, the
identities for $v_\infty$, $b$, $\Delta$ and $\theta_{\mathrm{s}}$, and the
form of the deflection map under explicit potential hypotheses are the
content of the mathematics and physics theorems of this page, not of this
definition.

Adopt a central scattering model of [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] clause (i)
with masses $m_1,m_2>0$, reduced mass $\mu=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$, static
central pair potential $u\in C^2((0,\infty))$
([[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and let $E>0$, $J>0$; write
$$V(r):=u(r)+\frac{J^2}{2\mu r^2}\qquad(r>0).$$
Suppose:

**(H1) finite range:** there is $R>0$ with $u(r)=0$ for every $r\ge R$;

**(H2) simple outer turning point:** there is $r_*>0$ with
$$V(r_*)=E,\qquad V'(r_*)<0,\qquad V(r)<E\quad(r>r_*).$$

Let $r:J_0\to\mathbb R^3$ be the relative coordinate of a motion of the model
on an interval $J_0$ with nonempty interior and with attached angular
momentum $j=\mu\,r\times r'=Je_3\ne0$ and attached energy $E$
([[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]],
[[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]]), and suppose
$|r(t)|\ge r_*$ for every $t\in J_0$ and $|r(t_*)|=r_*$ for some
$t_*\in J_0$. Then:

1. **(The scattering motion.)** $r$ extends uniquely to a central-force
   trajectory $\bar r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^3$ for $(\mu,u)$; the extension is
   the relative coordinate of a motion of the two-label model defined on all
   of $\mathbb R$, whose centre of mass is the affine extension of the
   original one. Along $\bar r$, $\rho:=|\bar r|$ satisfies $\rho\ge r_*$,
   $\rho(t)>r_*$ for $t\ne t_*$, and $\rho$ is strictly decreasing on
   $(-\infty,t_*]$ and strictly increasing on $[t_*,\infty)$; no collision
   occurs. Moreover the time quadrature
   $$\tau(r_0):=\int_{r_*}^{r_0}\frac{\mathrm ds}{\sqrt{(2/\mu)\bigl(E-V(s)\bigr)}}\qquad(r_0\ge r_*)$$
   is finite for every $r_0$ and satisfies $\rho(t_*\pm\tau(r_0))=r_0$.
2. **(Free asymptotes, speed and impact parameter.)** The limits
   $v_\pm=\lim_{t\to\pm\infty}\bar r'(t)$ exist and
   $$|v_+|=|v_-|=\sqrt{2E/\mu}=:v_\infty .$$
   For every $t_1\ge t_*$ with $\rho(t_1)\ge R$ the motion is exactly free
   from $t_1$ on, $\bar r(t)=\bar r(t_1)+(t-t_1)v_+$ for all $t\ge t_1$;
   symmetrically for the incoming branch with $v_-$. The perpendicular
   distance from the force centre of the incoming line and of the outgoing
   line is the same number
   $$b=\frac{J}{\mu v_\infty}=\frac{J}{\sqrt{2\mu E}},\qquad\text{so that}\qquad J=\mu b\,v_\infty .$$
3. **(Polar advance and deflection.)** Let $(\rho,\theta)$ be polar data of
   $r$ in an oriented orthonormal triad with $e_3=j/J$
   ([[thm-cm-central-force-polar-reduction]]). Then
   $$\Delta:=\theta(+\infty)-\theta(t_*)=\theta(t_*)-\theta(-\infty) =\int_{r_*}^{\infty}\frac{J\,\mathrm dr}{r^2\sqrt{2\mu\,\bigl(E-V(r)\bigr)}}$$
   is finite and positive, and the asymptotic directions satisfy
   $$\frac{v_+}{|v_+|}=-R_{2\Delta}\Bigl(\frac{v_-}{|v_-|}\Bigr),\qquad \frac{\langle v_-,v_+\rangle}{|v_-|\,|v_+|}=\cos(\pi-2\Delta),$$
   where $R_\alpha$ is the rotation of the plane
   $\operatorname{span}(e_1,e_2)$ by $\alpha$. The scattering angle of the
   motion is $\theta_{\mathrm s}=\arccos(\cos(\pi-2\Delta))$; if
   $0<\Delta<\pi/2$ then $\theta_{\mathrm s}=\pi-2\Delta\in(0,\pi)$ and the
   signed velocity rotation is $2\Delta-\pi$.
4. **(Cross-section of a deflection branch.)** Let
   $\theta:(a_1,a_2)\to(0,\pi)$ be a deflection branch of the model in the
   sense of [[def-cm15-cross-section]]: $\theta$ is $C^1$ with
   $\theta'(b)\ne0$, and for every $b\in(a_1,a_2)$ the scattering motion of
   the model with impact parameter $b$, energy $E$ and angular momentum
   $Je_3$ has scattering angle $\theta_{\mathrm s}(b)=\theta(b)$, with
   $0<\Delta(b)<\pi/2$. Then, for every continuous
   $2\pi$-periodic $g:(0,\pi)\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$,
   $$\int_{a_1}^{a_2}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi} g\bigl(\theta(b),\varphi\bigr)\;b\;\mathrm db\,\mathrm d\varphi =\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}\!\!\int_0^{2\pi} g(\theta,\varphi)\;b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|\;\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi,$$
   the outgoing angular measure of the branch has density
   $b(\theta)|b'(\theta)|$ with respect to $\mathrm d\theta\,\mathrm d\varphi$,
   and the differential cross-section of the branch is
   $$\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta) =\frac{b(\theta)\,\bigl|b'(\theta)\bigr|}{\sin\theta} =\frac{b(\theta)}{\sin\theta\,\bigl|\theta'(b(\theta))\bigr|}\qquad(\theta_1<\theta<\theta_2).$$
   Under the uniform-incident preparation of
   [[def-cm15-asymptotic-data]] clause (iv) with cutoff
   $b_{\max}\in(a_1,a_2]$ and flux $\Phi$, the model predicts the expected
   scattered rate
   $$\dot N=\Phi\,\sigma\bigl((\theta(a_1),\theta(b_{\max}))\bigr),\qquad \sigma(Y)=\int_Y\frac{\mathrm d\sigma}{\mathrm d\Omega}(\theta)\,2\pi\sin\theta\,\mathrm d\theta,$$
   into the corresponding window of scattering angles.
5. **(Scope of the statement.)** The theorem asserts nothing about the
   deflection map outside the recorded branch: it neither asserts that
   $b\mapsto\theta_{\mathrm s}$ is decreasing, injective or free of
   stationary points, nor that the branch images cover $(0,\pi)$; and it
   treats finite-range potentials only. The collisions, long-range
   potentials, velocity-dependent forces and external forces are excluded by
   the model class of [[post-cm05-central-model]] and by (H1).

derivations.claim: Motion: for $0<b<a$ the model of the Facts admits the exact broken-straight motion: an incoming straight line, a chord inside $r<a$ (the label moves freely there with speed $v_{\mathrm{in}}$), and an outgoing straight line; the entry and exit data are related by the two conservation rules as in [L1], and [L2] computes the outgoing direction. For $b>a$ the line misses the shell; at $b=a$ it has the adopted free grazing continuation. In both cases the deflection is $0$.
Deflection formula: by [L2], for $b\in(0,a)$ the angle between the incoming and outgoing directions is $\theta(b)=2(\alpha-\beta)$ with $\sin\alpha=b/a$ and $\sin\beta=\sin\alpha/n=b/(na)$, that is

Monotonicity: differentiating [L3], $$\theta'(b)=2\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{a^2-b^2}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{n^2a^2-b^2}}\right)>0\qquad(0<b<a),$$ because $n>1$ gives $\sqrt{n^2a^2-b^2}>\sqrt{a^2-b^2}>0$, so the first reciprocal exceeds the second; hence $\theta$ is strictly increasing on $(0,a)$, the opposite of the claimed decrease.

Consistency of the contact rule: at the entry the angular momentum about the centre is $\mu b v_\infty$, and inside it equals $\mu a v_{\mathrm{in}}\sin\beta=\mu a\,nv_\infty\sin\beta=\mu b v_\infty$, so angular momentum is conserved across the interface as the radial contact force requires; the energy is conserved by construction of $v_{\mathrm{in}}$ with $U_0=\frac54E$. This separate contact model is conservative and finite-range as an adopted radial rule; it is not a member of the smooth central-scattering class.

Values and the grazing jump: $\theta(0)=0$ and, as $b\uparrow a$, $\alpha\to\pi/2$ and $\beta\to\arcsin(1/n)=\arcsin\frac23$, so $\theta(b)\to\pi-2\arcsin\frac23\approx1.682$ rad $\approx96.4^\circ$; while for every $b\ge a$ the deflection is $0$. The map is therefore not decreasing (it increases on $(0,a)$ and then drops to $0$), and it is not injective: the value $0$ is attained for every $b\ge a$, in addition to its branch value at $b=0$.

Conclusion: step 1.3 refutes the stated global strict-decrease claim with a genuine smooth central-scattering model satisfying its positive-energy, nonzero-angular-momentum and unique-angle hypotheses. More generally, any finite-range model whose angle is defined for every positive impact parameter has the constant free tail established there, so global strict decrease fails even when the interaction inside the range is nontrivial. Steps 1.1-3.1 separately retain the increasing refracting-shell branch and its adopted grazing jump; that contact comparison lies outside the smooth class and supplies no claim that $C^2$ regularity implies or is necessary for monotonicity. The central-scattering theorem itself records no global monotonicity claim and assumes a chosen nondegenerate branch for its cross-section formula.

Genuine smooth finite-range witness and the general obstruction: fix an adopted smooth central model on time window $\mathbb R$ with $u(r)=0$ for $r\ge R$, and let $b>R$, $v_\infty=\sqrt{2E/\mu}$ and $r_b(t)=(v_\infty t,b,0)$. Then $|r_b(t)|\ge b>R$, so $u=u'=0$ along it and $r_b''=0$ solves the reduced equation. With $M=m_1+m_2$, the curves $x_1=(m_2/M)r_b$, $x_2=-(m_1/M)r_b$ have separation $r_b$, zero accelerations and zero force, hence are motions of the adopted model with zero centre of mass. Both asymptotic relative velocities equal $(v_\infty,0,0)$, so the deflection is uniquely $0$. Any incoming line with impact parameter $b>R$ stays outside the interaction region and continues freely; thus every finite-range model has this constant deflection tail. In particular $u=0$ is $C^2$ and finite-range, and the same construction works for every $b>0$, giving a unique angle $0$ for every positive impact parameter; two distinct positive parameters therefore violate the asserted strict decrease.

Let $N\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ and let $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable at every point of $I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Put $M:=\sum_{i}m_i>0$, $X:=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_ix_i$ and $\rho_i:=x_i-X$; all sums over $i$ range over $1,\dots,N$ (the index set $\{1,\dots,N\}$ of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are the Euclidean inner product and norm on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then:

1. $X$ and every $\rho_i$ are differentiable on $I$, with $X'=M^{-1}\sum_im_ix_i'$ and $\rho_i'=x_i'-X'$, and the identities $\sum_im_i\rho_i=0$ and $\sum_im_i\rho_i'=0$ hold on $I$;
2. for every $t\in I$, $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\sum_{i}m_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2;$$
3. if $N=2$, then with $r:=x_1-x_2$ and $\mu:=m_1m_2/M$ one has $\sum_im_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$ and hence $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$$ for every $t\in I$.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Fix a model of the force branch [[post-cm02-force-superposition]]: $N\ge1$
particle labels with fixed masses $m_{1},\dots,m_{N}>0$
([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_{0}\subseteq\mathbb
R$, an open configuration domain $Q\subseteq\mathbb R^{3N}$ with its collision
set removed when the model's force law is singular there
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and a force map
$$F:I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}\longrightarrow(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$$
with the standing continuity and state-local-Lipschitz hypotheses of clause
(iii) of that postulate. Fix one inertial frame of the model with adapted
coordinates $(t,x)$ ([[post-cm01-frames]]), and let $J\subseteq I_{0}$ be an
interval with nonempty interior ([[def-interval]]). All sums below range over
$i=1,\dots,N$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $u\times v$, $\langle u,v\rangle$
and $\lVert u\rVert_{2}$ are the cross product, the Euclidean inner product and
the Euclidean norm on $\mathbb R^{3}$ ([[def-cross-product-in-r3]],
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]).

**(a) Curve families and motions.** A **curve family** of the model is a map
$x:J\to Q$, $x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{N})$, of class $C^{2}$ on $J$
([[def-cm01-velocity-acceleration]]); its **coordinate velocities** are
$w_{i}:=x_{i}'$ on $J$, written $w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{N}):J\to(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$.
A curve family is a **motion** of the model when
$$m_{i}\ddot x_{i}(t)=F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr)\qquad(i=1,\dots,N,\ t\in J),$$
the notion of clause (c) of [[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]. Every quantity of
this definition is defined for an arbitrary curve family; the balance theorems
of this page state which of their properties use the equations of motion.
Along a curve family the force map is evaluated at $(t,x(t),w(t))\in
I_{0}\times Q\times(\mathbb R^{3})^{N}$; when the model invokes the
external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of [[post-cm02-interactions]],
the maps $F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}$ and $F_{ij}$ are evaluated at their declared
arguments on the motion's state graph, where the presentation is an identity
for $F_{i}$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define
$$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$
Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$
the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$.
The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$
([[def-cm01-units]]). Since $x_{i}$ is $C^{2}$, each $p_{i}$ is $C^{1}$ and
each of $P$, $X$, $\rho_{i}$ is differentiable, as a finite sum of
differentiable curves ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]); write
$$V:=X'$$
for the **centre-of-mass velocity**. The algebraic identities
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\rho_{i}=0$, $P=MV$ and the splitting of the kinetic sum
$\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}\rVert_{2}^{2}$ are proved in the kinetic-splitting
theorem of this page; they are not part of this definition.

**(c) Angular momentum, torque, internal torque sum.** Let a **reference
curve** $o:J\to\mathbb R^{3}$ of class $C^{1}$ be given: a point about which
moments are taken, allowed to move (a constant map $o\equiv o_{0}$ is the
fixed-origin case). Define the **angular momentum about $o$** and the **total
torque about $o$** by
$$J_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times p_{i}(t),\qquad T_{o}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),$$
with dimensions $[J_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$ (read in
$\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m^{2}\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and
$[T_{o}]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in $\mathrm N\,\mathrm m$). When the
model invokes the external-plus-pair presentation of clause (i) of
[[post-cm02-interactions]], define in addition the **external torque** and the
**internal torque sum**
$$T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-o(t)\bigr)\times F_{i}^{\mathrm{ext}}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),w_{i}(t)\bigr),\qquad I(t):=\sum_{i<j}\bigl(x_{i}(t)-x_{j}(t)\bigr)\times F_{ij}\bigl(t,x_{i}(t),x_{j}(t),w_{i}(t),w_{j}(t)\bigr).$$
The sum $I$ does not involve $o$; it is defined whenever the pair
presentation is declared. The identity $T_{o}=T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}+I$ uses the
antisymmetry $F_{ji}=-F_{ij}$ of clause (ii)1 of that postulate to reindex the
ordered pairs and is proved as step 1.1 of the angular-momentum balance of
this page.

**(d) Kinetic energy, power, work.** Define the **kinetic energy** and the
**power of the total force** along the curve family by
$$K(t):=\frac12\sum_{i}m_{i}\lVert w_{i}(t)\rVert_{2}^{2},\qquad \mathcal P(t):=\sum_{i}\bigl\langle F_{i}\bigl(t,x(t),w(t)\bigr),\,w_{i}(t)\bigr\rangle,$$
of dimensions $[K]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules) and
$[\mathcal P]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-3}$ (read in watts), and for
$t_{0}<t_{1}$ in $J$ the **work of the total force** over $[t_{0},t_{1}]$ by
$$W([t_{0},t_{1}]):=\int_{t_{0}}^{t_{1}}\mathcal P(t)\,dt,$$
of dimension $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$ (read in joules); $\mathcal P$ is
continuous on $J$ because $F$, $x$ and $w$ are continuous, so the Riemann
integral exists ([[thm-continuous-implies-integrable]], see the page
`the-riemann-integral`). The **potential energy** is not defined by this item:
it belongs to the potential branch of the model and is defined in the
potential-and-mechanical-energy item of this page.

**(e) Frame and reference-point dependence.** The quantities $p_{i}$, $P$,
$X$, $\rho_{i}$, $V$, $K$, $\mathcal P$ and $W$ are read in the one inertial
frame fixed above, and $J_{o}$, $T_{o}$, $T_{o}^{\mathrm{ext}}$, $I$ are read
about the reference curve $o$ in that frame. They are not invariant under a
change of frame or reference point: their transformation laws under a change
of inertial frame are stated and proved in the frame-transformation item of
this page, and every conservation statement involving them names the frame
and the reference point in which it is made.

**(f) Status.** This item is a definition: it introduces symbols, their
domains, regularity, dimensions and frame dependence from the model's data.
It adopts no force law beyond the force branch already fixed, asserts no
balance of any of these quantities and records no measured value.

Adopt, as the **central-force model** for the two-body part of this page, the
following restricted model class inside the force and interaction branches of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] and [[post-cm02-interactions]].

**(i) The two-label central model.** A model of class (i) is a force model of
[[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=2$ labels, fixed masses
$m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), a time window $I_0$, the
collision-excluded configuration domain
$$Q:=\{\,x=(x_1,x_2)\in(\mathbb R^3)^2:\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert\in J_0\,\}$$
for an open interval $J_0\subseteq(0,\infty)$
([[def-cm01-configuration]]), and the force map presented through the
time-independent **static central pair potential**
$$U(x_1,x_2):=u(\lvert x_1-x_2\rvert),\qquad u:J_0\to\mathbb R\ \text{of class }C^2,$$
so that $F_i(t,x,v)=-\nabla_{x_i}U(x)$ on the state domain (clauses (iii)
and (iv) of [[post-cm02-interactions]]; $U$ is of class $C^2$ on the open
$Q$ by [[lem-cm05-radial-potential-gradient]]). In the external-plus-pair
presentation of clause (i) of that postulate the model has
$F_i^{\mathrm{ext}}\equiv0$: no external forces act on the labels of a model
of class (i).

**(ii) The reduced one-label problem.** For a model of class (i) put
$\mu:=m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)>0$ of dimension $\mu$ ([[def-cm01-units]]). The
**reduced problem** of the model is the one-label problem of mass $\mu$ whose
unknown is the relative coordinate $r=x_1-x_2$ and whose equation is
$$\mu\,r''=-\frac{u'(\lvert r\rvert)}{\lvert r\rvert}\,r;$$
by [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]] the relative coordinate of every motion
of a model of class (i) solves this equation, and every pair of a uniform
centre-of-mass motion and a solution of the reduced equation on a common
interval reconstructs a motion of the model. Adopt the reduced problem as the
object that the central-force statements of this page describe, and the
central-force-trajectory vocabulary of
[[def-cm-central-force-trajectory]] (attached angular momentum
$j=\mu\,r\times r'$ and energy $E=\tfrac12\mu\lVert r'\rVert_2^2+u(\lvert
r\rvert)$) as the vocabulary in which those statements are phrased.

**(iii) The one-label fixed-centre idealization.** A **one-label central
model** is a force model of [[post-cm02-force-superposition]] with $N=1$,
mass $\mu>0$, time window $I_0$, a fixed **centre** $c\in\mathbb R^3$, the
configuration domain $Q_c=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:\lvert x-c\rvert\in J_0\}$, and
the external force map
$$F(t,x,v)=-\frac{u'(\lvert x-c\rvert)}{\lvert x-c\rvert}\,(x-c),$$
presented through the potential $u(\lvert x-c\rvert)$ with the same function
$u\in C^2(J_0)$. This model is the **fixed-centre idealization** of the
reduced problem: it drops the centre-of-mass degree of freedom and holds the
force centre fixed. It is a separate adopted model class, not a consequence
of class (i), and every use of it must state that the idealization is
intended.

**(iv) Reading conventions.** In the statements of this page: the **force
centre** of the reduced problem is the origin of the relative coordinate
$r$; an **orbit** is the trajectory $t\mapsto r(t)$ of the reduced problem
(equivalently, by [[pthm-cm05-relative-reduction]], the trajectory of either
label relative to the centre of mass, up to the mass ratio); "circular" and
"elliptic" name properties of that trajectory; and the words "planet",
"satellite", "central body" and "test particle" name labels of a model of
class (i) or (iii). These words carry no empirical claim about nature.

**(v) Exclusions and status.** The class excludes: velocity-dependent and
explicitly time-dependent central forces; non-central and non-potential
forces; constraints and reaction forces; colliding configurations
$x_1=x_2$ (equivalently $r=0$); external forces on the labels; and models
with more than two labels. Finite-size, rotational, deformational, dissipative
and relativistic effects are outside the class. The masses, the interval
$J_0$ and the function $u$ (including any parameters it carries) are model
data, not measured values ([[def-cm01-units]]); quantitative empirical use
requires separately stated measured inputs with their uncertainties, and no
statement of this page asserts that any physical system is exactly a model
of this class.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-ordered-field]]) with its order
([[def-real-order]]).

A subset $I \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is **order-convex** when

$$x, y \in I \text{ and } x \le z \le y \;\Longrightarrow\; z \in I .$$

The **intervals** of $\mathbb{R}$ are the sets of the following nine forms, where
$a, b \in \mathbb{R}$:

| | bounded forms | | one-sided and full forms |
|---|---|---|---|
| $(a,b)$ | $\{x : a < x < b\}$ | $(a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a < x\}$ |
| $[a,b]$ | $\{x : a \le x \le b\}$ | $[a,\infty)$ | $\{x : a \le x\}$ |
| $[a,b)$ | $\{x : a \le x < b\}$ | $(-\infty,b)$ | $\{x : x < b\}$ |
| $(a,b]$ | $\{x : a < x \le b\}$ | $(-\infty,b]$ | $\{x : x \le b\}$ |
| | | $(-\infty,\infty)$ | $\mathbb{R}$ |

An interval is **open** when both of its written endpoints are excluded, that is
for the forms $(a,b)$, $(a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b)$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$; it is
**closed** when both written endpoints are included, that is for $[a,b]$,
$[a,\infty)$, $(-\infty,b]$ and $(-\infty,\infty)$. The forms $[a,b)$ and
$(a,b]$ are **half-open**.

**The symbols $\pm\infty$ are notation and not elements of $\mathbb{R}$.** They
mark which side carries no endpoint condition at all; the five forms in the right
column are defined by the displayed conditions on $x$ alone, and no arithmetic is
ever performed with $\infty$. This is the same refusal to extend $\mathbb{R}$
silently that [[rem-sup-conventions]] records for suprema.

**Every one of the nine forms is order-convex.** Each is defined by a conjunction
of at most two conditions, each of the shape $a < x$, $a \le x$, $x < b$ or
$x \le b$, and each such condition is inherited by an intermediate point: if
$a < x$ and $x \le z$ then $a < z$, and if $z \le y$ and $y < b$ then $z < b$,
by transitivity of the order ([[def-ordered-field]]). Applying this to whichever
one or two conditions define the form in question gives $z \in I$ whenever
$x, y \in I$ and $x \le z \le y$.

**Bounded intervals.** An interval is **bounded** ([[def-bounded-set]]) exactly
when it is of one of the four forms in the left column: for those, $a$ is a lower
bound and $b$ an upper bound. The other five forms are unbounded, on the side or
sides written with $\infty$; the verification is in the remarks below.

**Nondegeneracy.** An interval is **degenerate** when it has at most one element,
and **nondegenerate** when it has at least two. For the four bounded forms with
endpoints $a$ and $b$:

- $[a,b]$ is nonempty exactly when $a \le b$, and it is nondegenerate exactly
  when $a < b$. It is the singleton $\{a\}$ when $a = b$.
- $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are nonempty exactly when $a < b$, and then each
  is nondegenerate.

The only assertion here that is not immediate from the defining conditions is
that $a < b$ makes $(a,b)$ nonempty with at least two points. It holds because
$a < (a+b)/2 < b$, which follows from $a < b$ by adding $a$, respectively $b$, to
both sides and halving ([[def-ordered-field]]); repeating the halving inside
$(a, (a+b)/2)$ produces a second point.

**Closed bounded intervals.** These are the sets $[a,b]$ with $a \le b$, which is
exactly the condition making them nonempty. They are the intervals the nested
interval property is stated for, and the phrase *closed bounded interval* always
carries the hypothesis $a \le b$ in this library.

**Length.** The **length** of a bounded interval presented by its endpoints
$a \le b$ is

$$\ell = b - a \;\ge\; 0 .$$

Length is attached to the presentation by endpoints and is not recovered from the
set: $(a,b)$, $[a,b)$ and $(a,b]$ are all empty when $a = b$, and so is
$(c,c)$ for any other $c$, while each of these presentations has length $0$, so
nothing inconsistent arises; but the endpoints are named explicitly at every
point where a length is used in this library, and never inferred from the set.
Unbounded intervals are assigned no length.

Substitution yields $Mv_1^++m_2d^+=MV$, hence $v_1^+=V+(m_2/M)ed^-$ and $v_2^+=V-(m_1/M)ed^-$. These vectors satisfy both equations, so they are the unique outcome of the hypothetical law. The declared potential is identically zero, hence unchanged across the continuous configuration. Consequently $\Delta(K+U)=3\,\mathrm J>0$, which refutes the universal across-impact conservation assertion. Both positions are continuous, their derivatives are the stated velocities, their accelerations vanish off zero, and the separation is $1-2t>0$ before zero and $1+4t>0$ after zero. Therefore allowing every real $e$ does not give a conservative contact law for the two-label mechanical-energy account; it requires an additional energy input if conservation of an enlarged account is imposed. citations.quote: **(i) The isolated reciprocal impulse model.** A two-label force model with masses $m_1,m_2>0$ ([[post-cm01-worldlines]] clause (v)), time window $I_0$, configuration domain $Q$ ([[def-cm01-configuration]]) and continuous external-plus-pair force maps $F_1,F_2$ is **run in the isolated reciprocal impulse model at $t_*\in I_0$** when there is a motion $x=(x_1,x_2):I\to Q$ of the associated first-order system ([[def-cm02-newtonian-flow]]) such that: 1. $x_1,x_2$ are continuous on $I$ and twice continuously differentiable on each of $I\cap(-\infty,t_*)$ and $I\cap(t_*,\infty)$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]]), and $m_ix_i''(t)=F_i(t,x(t),x'(t))$ for every $t\in I\setminus\{t_*\}$; 2. the one-sided limits $v_i^{\pm}:=\lim_{t\to t_*\pm}x_i'(t)$ exist in $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-vector-valued-functions-limits-and-continuity]]); 3. there is a vector $J\in\mathbb R^3$, the **impulse**, with $$m_1\bigl(v_1^+-v_1^-\bigr)=J,\qquad m_2\bigl(v_2^+-v_2^-\bigr)=-J .$$ The two equations of clause 3 are the **reciprocal finite-jump form** of the isolated impulse: the two labels receive equal and opposite momentum changes. The model places no bound on the force maps across $t_*$; its distributional rendering by test-function pairings is proved in [[thm-cm-impulse-restitution-and-energy-loss]]. The dimension of the impulse is $[J]=\mathsf M\ell\tau^{-1}$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

1. **(Momentum continuity.)** The total momentum is continuous across the impact, $$P(t_*^+)=P(t_*^-),\qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad \sum_{i=1}^2 m_i\bigl(v_i^+-v_i^-\bigr)=0,$$ and the impulse delivered to label $1$ is removed from label $2$: $J=m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=-m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)$.

Let $N\ge1$, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval with at least two points ([[def-interval]]), let $m_1,\dots,m_N>0$ and let $x_i:I\to\mathbb R^3$ be differentiable at every point of $I$ ([[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]]). Put $M:=\sum_{i}m_i>0$, $X:=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_ix_i$ and $\rho_i:=x_i-X$; all sums over $i$ range over $1,\dots,N$ (the index set $\{1,\dots,N\}$ of [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]), and $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$, $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are the Euclidean inner product and norm on $\mathbb R^3$ ([[def-euclidean-inner-product]]). Then: 1. $X$ and every $\rho_i$ are differentiable on $I$, with $X'=M^{-1}\sum_im_ix_i'$ and $\rho_i'=x_i'-X'$, and the identities $\sum_im_i\rho_i=0$ and $\sum_im_i\rho_i'=0$ hold on $I$; 2. for every $t\in I$, $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\sum_{i}m_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2;$$ 3. if $N=2$, then with $r:=x_1-x_2$ and $\mu:=m_1m_2/M$ one has $\sum_im_i\lVert\rho_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$ and hence $$\sum_{i}m_i\lVert x_i'(t)\rVert_2^2=M\lVert X'(t)\rVert_2^2+\mu\lVert r'(t)\rVert_2^2$$ for every $t\in I$.

**(b) Total mass, total momentum, centre of mass, relative positions.** Define $$M:=\sum_{i}m_{i}>0,\qquad p_{i}:=m_{i}w_{i},\qquad P(t):=\sum_{i}p_{i}(t),\qquad X(t):=M^{-1}\sum_{i}m_{i}x_{i}(t),\qquad \rho_{i}:=x_{i}-X.$$ Here $p_{i}$ is the **momentum** of label $i$, $P$ the **total momentum**, $X$ the **centre of mass** and $\rho_{i}$ the **relative position** of label $i$. The dimensions are $[M]=\mu$, $[p_{i}]=[P]=\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$ (read in $\mathrm{kg}\,\mathrm m\,\mathrm s^{-1}$) and $[X]=[\rho_{i}]=\ell$ ([[def-cm01-units]]).

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number $$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$ the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$ (extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The **Euclidean norm** of $x$ is $$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$ which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and [[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by [[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

derivations.claim: Common data: $M=8$, $\mu=\frac32$, $V=\frac{2\cdot3+6\cdot(-1)}{8}=0$, $d^-=-4n$, $\lVert d^-\rVert_2^2=16$, $K^-=12\ \mathrm{J}$.
Outcome (a), sticking: $v_1^+=v_2^+=0$. Then $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=2(0-3)n=-6n$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=6(0+1)n=+6n$; the impulse is $J=-6n\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ and the total momentum is $0=P^-$.
Outcome (b), elastic: $v_1^+=-3n$, $v_2^+=+1n$. Then $m_1(v_1^+-v_1^-)=2(-6)n=-12n$ and $m_2(v_2^+-v_2^-)=6(+2)n=+12n$; the impulse is $J=-12n\ \mathrm{N\,s}$ and the total momentum is $0=P^-$.

Both outcomes satisfy the reciprocal impulse equations of [L1], with different impulses ($-6n$ versus $-12n$), and the same given incoming data; their post-impact velocities differ ($0$ versus $-3n$ and $+1n$). Hence the impulse equations alone do not fix the post-impact velocities, and the false statement fails.

Energy: by [L2] the changes are $\Delta K_{(a)}=\frac32\cdot\frac12(0-16)=-12\ \mathrm{J}$ and $\Delta K_{(b)}=\frac32\cdot\frac12(16-16)=0$; the outcomes are therefore also distinguished by their energy accounting, so no choice of impulse can be recovered from the momentum data and the two outcomes are genuinely different model histories.

Consequence: in the collinear isolated-impact model the contact law of [[post-cm15-impulse]] clause (ii) (equivalently, the coefficient $e$, or a dynamical contact model producing the impulse) is an independent model datum; the reciprocal impulse equations constrain only the *sum* $m_1\Delta v_1+m_2\Delta v_2=0$. The same conclusion is recorded as clause 5 of [[pthm-cm15-impact-balance]].
